### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Johnson and Zhang deliver something the campus-speech literature did not have: a hand-built, 35-year record of 1,875 commencement speaker-institution-years at 52 U.S. universities, each speaker classified as liberal or conservative from FEC contribution records (or party affiliation for elected officials). On that foundation the paper establishes three things a reader can take away with ordinary caveats: among the 1,353 classifiable speakers at these institutions, liberals outnumber conservatives roughly three to one; the liberal share rose over 1989–2024 (a full-period slope of 0.0044 per year, SE 0.0011, that does not depend on any contested modeling choice); and public institutions invite conservative speakers markedly more often than private ones (about 19 percentage points), the paper's largest and most stable regression estimate. Beyond that descriptive core, the inferential and interpretive layers run ahead of the design. The pooled logit on 52 institutions reports no clustering and no year control in a window where the outcome and several covariates trend together; the two most quotable environmental findings — that disinvitation campaigns shift speaker selection and that the model explains 62% of the time trend — rest on a decay parameter tuned to the outcome and on coefficient attenuation from co-trending regressors, and are then narrated in causal language the cross-sectional design cannot carry; the endowment result cited in the Introduction and Discussion is null in the only reported table; and the paper describes its central measure two incompatible ways (a lifetime donation aggregate versus a time-specific one), which matters for how much of the post-2011 acceleration reflects changing invitations versus changing donor detectability on a shrinking classifiable denominator. Verification is further limited by the absence of code, a replication package, or a documented FEC-matching protocol despite fully public inputs. The field should adopt this paper as the reference for the descriptive facts about commencement speaker partisanship at selective four-year institutions, cite the sector and curricular gradients as robust associations, and treat the disinvitation, state-politics, and organizational-strategy claims as hypotheses the data motivate rather than findings they establish.

#### Key Strengths

- A genuinely novel empirical object: 1,875 speaker-institution-years across 52 institutions and 35 years, compiled from institutional listings, archivists, and public relations staff and hand-matched to FEC records — an archival, behavioral measure of a routine organizational practice in a literature that has relied almost entirely on attitude surveys and case studies of individual controversies.
- Transparent, auditable sample construction. Table 2 accounts for every one of the 1,875 observations (1,043 liberal, 310 conservative, 233 no contribution, 91 foreign, 163 neutrality-norm occupations, 35 unclear), the arithmetic reproduces exactly, and the exclusions are named and justified; the 50%-rule classification is carried through a stricter two-thirds rule (Appendix A4) and a mixed-effects specification (A5) with consistent results.
- Two findings that are large, stable across specifications, and substantively informative: the ~19-percentage-point higher probability of a conservative speaker at public institutions (which complicates the flat 'universities platform liberals' narrative by showing it varies by sector), and the negative association between occupational/professional enrollment share and liberal speakers (a fresh correlate linking speaker selection to Brint et al.'s curricular-change literature).
- A candid Methods section. The convenience-plus-purposive sampling is disclosed and its tilt toward well-resourced coastal and AAU institutions acknowledged; the 'Conceptualizing Political Orientation' subsection bounds the liberal/conservative labels to contemporary U.S. partisan alignment and explicitly disclaims speaker orientation as a proxy for institutional ideology; and the exclusion of neutrality-norm occupations is checked for trend (Figures 3–4).

#### Key Concerns

- Inference is under-specified for the regressors the paper foregrounds. Standard errors in Table 4 are not clustered (the word does not appear in the paper) even though four regressors are constant within the 52 institutions and four vary only at the state-year level; there is no year control despite a 35-year window in which the outcome, racial-composition shares, enrollment, and disinvitation counts all trend. The p < .05 and p < .10 results — location, yield rate, occupational majors, Hispanic share, state party control, and both disinvitation terms — are the ones a clustering correction or year control could plausibly move.
- The headline time-trend rests on a measure and a denominator that both change over the window. The paper says in consecutive sentences that classification uses donations aggregated across 1989–2024 (so a 1993 speaker may be labeled by 2016 gifts) and that it uses time-specific contributions capturing positioning at the moment of selection; these cannot both be true. Separately, the classifiable share shrinks late in the period (the no-contribution group grows) and the propensity to appear in FEC records as a Democratic donor rose sharply after 2010 for reasons unrelated to universities. The direction of the trend is very likely real; its magnitude and the sharpness of the 2011 break are not pinned down.
- Two tuned parameters are tested as if pre-specified. The 0.8 decay factor on lagged disinvitation counts was selected by testing which value best predicted the outcome, and the 2010/2011 break point was estimated from the same series whose post-break slope is then reported at p < .05; both nominal significance levels are optimistic (the slope difference is roughly t = 2.1 before any adjustment). The disinvitation coefficients, which also co-trend with the outcome and lack a year control, are then narrated as evidence that campaigns 'influence' institutional behavior.
- The prose outruns the exhibits in the sections most readers rely on. The endowment finding stated in the Introduction and Discussion is null in Table 4 (0.034, SE 0.026) and comes from an unreported model that drops public/private control, the strongest predictor; 'more racially diverse student bodies' compresses a precise null for Black share (0.215, SE 1.826) and a p < .10 Hispanic result; the '62% of the time trend explained' figure is attenuation of a year coefficient by co-trending covariates, not a decomposition; and the abstract's 1,875 overstates the analytic N of 1,353. There is no limitations section, and causal verbs ('shape,' 'influence,' 'drive,' 'shifts') appear throughout the abstract and Discussion for a pooled cross-sectional logit.
- The study is not verifiable as published despite using only public inputs. There is no data availability statement, replication package, or code; the FEC name-matching procedure — the core measurement — has no stated rule, threshold, or reliability check; it is unclear whether the appendix publishes each speaker's classification or the speaker-by-institution-year roster; the imputation model for the ~20% missing citizen ideology is unspecified; and two reported results (the 62% claim and the endowment model) have no exhibit anywhere. The literature review also omits the campaign-finance ideology-scaling literature (Bonica's DIME/CFscores) that is the direct methodological antecedent, and misstates that no reliable strategy exists for scoring judges' ideology.

#### What to Rely On

- Among classifiable commencement speakers at these 52 institutions, liberal-classified speakers substantially outnumber conservative ones (1,043 vs. 310; 77%/23% under the majority rule, 75%/22%/3% independent under the two-thirds rule).
- The liberal share of classifiable speakers rose over 1989–2024: full-period slope 0.0044 per year (SE 0.0011), a result that survives every classification and specification choice the paper reports. The direction of a post-2010 acceleration is well supported even if its precise timing and magnitude are not.
- Public institutions in this sample are markedly more likely to invite conservative speakers than private ones — a marginal effect of about 19 percentage points (coef. −1.220, SE 0.354), robust across the 50% and two-thirds rules and the mixed-effects specification, and large enough to survive any plausible clustering correction.
- Institutions with larger occupational/professional enrollment shares invite fewer liberal speakers (ME −0.230 per unit share, i.e., about 2.3 points per 10-point change), and institutions in states with more liberal citizen ideology invite more liberal speakers (ME 0.054 per SD, p < .001, with enough margin to likely survive clustering). Cite both as associations.
- The methodological existence proof: a routine, universally observed organizational practice around campus speech can be studied with archival behavioral data matched to public records, rather than through attitude surveys and case studies of controversies. This is the paper's most durable conceptual contribution.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- That disinvitation campaigns 'influence' or 'shift' speaker selection — the decay parameter was tuned to the outcome, the coefficients are unclustered, there is no year control, and left-initiated attempts and the liberal speaker share rise over the same years; read as descriptive co-movement, not an effect of organized pressure on institutional behavior.
- The '62% of the time trend explained' figure — it is the shrinkage of a year coefficient when co-trending covariates are added (0.0044 to 0.0017), which is collinearity rather than mechanism; do not cite it as the share of the shift attributable to organizational or environmental factors.
- The precise 2010/2011 break point and the post-2011 slope of 0.0121 — the break was estimated from the data and tested as if known, the two segment slopes differ at only about t = 2.1, the post-2011 segment has 14 annual points, and the classifiable denominator shifts in exactly that window.
- That larger endowments predict liberal speakers — the endowment coefficient in Table 4 is null (0.034, SE 0.026); the significant result quoted in the Introduction and Discussion comes from an unreported model that drops public/private control, the paper's strongest predictor.
- That 'more racially diverse student bodies' predict liberal speakers — Black share is a precise null (0.215, SE 1.826), Hispanic share is p < .10, and only Asian share clears p < .05; name Asian (and, tentatively, Hispanic) share specifically, and convert the marginal effects (1.491 and 0.817 are per full 0-to-1 unit of a proportion, roughly 1.5 and 0.8 points per percentage point of enrollment).
- The state party control result (0.399, p < .10) and the selectivity results (yield rate −2.093 at p < .05; admission rate insignificant with the opposite sign) — the first is null-adjacent before any clustering correction, and the second uses 2022 IPEDS values projected back to 1989 with two proxies pointing in opposite directions.
- The 77%/23% split or any level estimate as a statistic about U.S. higher education — the 52 institutions are a convenience-plus-purposive draw seeded from the AAU, concentrated in the Northeast and on the coasts, with 32 doctoral institutions, no community colleges, four public master's institutions, and no HBCUs or HSIs.
- The framing of universities as 'strategic organizations navigating legitimacy' and of speaker selection as 'permeable to organized external pressure' — no decision process, administrator, or deliberation is observed; these are interpretive frames placed on cross-sectional correlations, and the paper's own future-research section concedes qualitative work is needed to establish them.
- The description of the ideology measure as 'time-specific' — the paper also states it is a lifetime aggregate over 1989–2024, and the operational rule described (share of a person's contributions to one party) implies the aggregate reading; assume the static version, which means early-period speakers may be classified by much later donations.
- The claim that 'no systematic or reliable strategy' exists for inferring the ideology of judges and journalists, and the 'first systematic longitudinal evidence' novelty claim — campaign-finance-based judicial ideology scores are standard in political science, and advocacy tallies of commencement-speaker partisanship predate this paper; the defensible claim is the first peer-reviewed, multi-institution, covariate-adjusted longitudinal analysis.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper rests on an unusually laborious and genuinely novel data-collection effort — 1,875 hand-compiled commencement speaker-institution-years across 35 years, individually matched to FEC contribution records — and the descriptive core (liberal speakers predominate, rose over time, and are markedly less common at public institutions) is well supported. The inferential layer is weaker than the data layer: the pooled logit gives no evidence of clustered standard errors despite 52 institutions and several institution-level, time-invariant regressors; the main model contains no year control in a 35-year window where both the outcome and several key covariates trend strongly; and two tuning parameters (the 0.8 decay factor and the 2010/2011 break point) were selected on the same outcome and then tested with conventional p-values. Readers should treat the descriptive time series and the large public/private contrast as solid, and the state-environment and disinvitation coefficients as suggestive associations rather than the causal influences the Discussion describes.

**Strengths:**

- The data-collection effort is the paper's real methodological contribution and is hard to fault: 1,875 speaker-institution-years across 52 institutions and 36 years, assembled from institutional listings supplemented by direct work with archivists and public relations officers, then matched speaker-by-speaker to FEC records on last name, first name, middle initial, and occupational history, with home-address corroboration used to resolve ambiguous matches. Nothing comparable exists in the campus-speech literature, which has relied almost entirely on attitudinal surveys and episodic case studies.
- Measurement decisions are unusually transparent and auditable. Table 2 reports the full disposition of all 1,875 observations, so a reader can reconstruct exactly why 522 fall out of the analytic sample (233 with no FEC record, 163 in occupations with neutrality norms, 91 foreign nationals, 35 unresolvable matches) and verify that 1,875 - 522 = the N = 1,353 in Table 4. The 50% classification rule is stated plainly, and a stricter two-thirds rule with an explicit independent category is carried through as a reported robustness check (Appendix Table A4).
- The authors run the one falsification check most directly available to them for their largest discretionary exclusion: Figures 3 and 4 tabulate the 'unique occupation' speakers (journalists, judges, clergy, military) by year and show stable counts with no trend, which does meaningfully reduce the worry that excluding them manufactures the time trend.
- The choice of a pooled specification over institution fixed effects is defended on substantive rather than convenient grounds and the defense is correct: institution FE would absorb public/private control, location, and selectivity, which are the variables RQ2 is actually about, and several time-varying covariates have limited within-institution variation. A mixed-effects logit with institution random intercepts is estimated as an alternative (Appendix Table A5) and reported as consistent.
- Estimation mechanics for the missing-data problem are handled with the right tools: 20 multiple imputations via Stata's mi estimate, with marginal effects computed through mimrgns so that Rubin's rules propagate imputation uncertainty into the reported standard errors rather than treating imputed values as observed.

**Weaknesses:**

- No clustering of standard errors is documented anywhere. The words 'cluster' and 'robust standard errors' do not appear in the paper, and the Table 4 note describes only multiple imputation and mimrgns. This matters most for the institution-level, time-invariant regressors — public institution (coef. -1.220, ME -0.186), location (-0.362), admission rate, yield rate (-2.093) — whose effective sample size is 52 institutions, not the 1,353 rows the standard errors are apparently computed from. The state-level regressors (party control, citizen ideology, both disinvitation counts) are worse still: they vary only at the state-year level across roughly 40-odd states, a textbook Moulton setup. The reported stars on the marginal-p<.05 results (yield rate, location, occupational majors, and both disinvitation terms) should be discounted accordingly.
- Table 4 contains no year variable. In a sample spanning 1989-2024, the outcome trends upward and so do several regressors — percent Hispanic students, percent Asian students, log enrollment, and both state disinvitation counts all rose substantially over this period for reasons having nothing to do with commencement. Any of these can correlate with the outcome purely through a shared time trend. The authors clearly ran year-controlled models (the decomposition exercise requires them) but report only the marginal effect of year from those runs, never the covariate coefficients. A reader who wants to know whether the percent-Asian result survives a year control cannot find out from the paper.
- The '62% of the time trend explained' decomposition does not support the interpretation placed on it. Adding covariates drops the marginal effect of year from 0.0044 to a non-significant 0.0017; post-2011 it falls from 0.0121 to 0.0066. This demonstrates that the covariates are collinear with time, which is guaranteed given that several of them are trending variables. It is not evidence that those covariates are the mechanism generating the trend, and the Discussion's reading ('organizational and environmental factors drive a substantial share of the change') asserts causal content the exercise cannot deliver.
- Both tuning parameters were selected on the same outcome they are then used to test. The 0.8 decay factor is chosen by testing 'various decay factors to assess how well this variable predicted commencement speakers' political ideologies' — an explicit fit-maximizing search — after which the resulting coefficients (0.129 and -0.183, both nominally p<.05, t ≈ 2.5 and 2.1) are reported with conventional standard errors that ignore the search. Similarly, the 2010/2011 break point is 'estimated through the model-fitting process' and the post-break slope (0.0121, SE 0.0047) is then tested as if the break date were known a priori; estimated break points require non-standard (sup-Wald) critical values. In both cases the nominal significance is optimistic.
- The political-orientation measure is internally contradictory as described. Page 14 first states the classification 'is based on each speaker's aggregated political donations between 1989 and 2024 and therefore does not capture potential changes in their political orientations over time' — i.e., one time-invariant label per person — and then immediately claims that 'because we measure political orientation using time-specific campaign contributions, our operationalization captures speakers' positioning relative to the political landscape at the moment of selection.' Both cannot be true. The aggregation rule described in the methods implies the former, meaning a speaker who appeared in 1993 may be classified by donations made in 2016.
- The 'no contribution' exclusion is not subjected to the same trend check as the occupation exclusion, and the paper states outright that this group grew: 'The number of speakers with no political contributions also increased late in the study period.' The classified denominator therefore shrinks precisely in the window (post-2011) where the trend accelerates. Because Figures 5 and 6 plot the liberal share among the classifiable only, a compositional shift in who is classifiable can move that share without any change in underlying selection behavior. No bounding exercise is offered, and the direction of the resulting bias cannot be signed from the text.
- Institutional control, location, admission rate, and yield rate are all drawn from the 2022 IPEDS files and applied unchanged to 1989-2024, justified on the grounds that selectivity fluctuations 'likely reflect year-to-year variations rather than real changes in selectivity.' That is defensible for control and location but not for selectivity over a 35-year window in which admission rates at highly selective institutions fell by a factor of three or more. The yield-rate result (ME -0.320, the second-largest effect in Table 4) is best understood as a 2020s institutional-prestige ranking projected backwards, not as a measure of contemporaneous selectivity.
- The multiple imputation is reported but not documented. Citizen ideology is missing for roughly 20% of cases and the Berry et al. series has known coverage limits at the ends of its range, so the missingness is plausibly concentrated in specific years rather than scattered at random. The imputation model is not described, no MAR justification is given, and no complete-case comparison is shown. Since citizen ideology carries one of the paper's strongest results (0.356, p<.001) and enters the trend decomposition, readers cannot assess how much of that estimate depends on imputed values.
- Two claims in the abstract and Discussion are not supported by the primary model. The endowment finding ('universities with... larger endowments' tend liberal) is not significant in Table 4 (0.034, SE 0.026); it becomes significant only in an unreported auxiliary specification that drops public/private control — that is, a specification that removes the strongest confounder. And 'more racially diverse student bodies' compresses a heterogeneous set of results: percent Asian (p<.01) and percent Hispanic (p<.10) are positive, but percent Black is 0.215 with SE 1.826, an estimate indistinguishable from zero and too imprecise to sign.
- The Discussion's verbs consistently exceed the design. 'Disinvitation efforts influence institutional behavior,' 'organized political pressure influences speaker selection,' 'the ideological direction of disinvitation campaigns in a state shifts institutional behavior,' and 'platform allocation decisions are systematically shaped by external political environments' all describe causal effects. The estimating equation is a pooled cross-sectional logit with no institution fixed effects, no year fixed effects, no instrument, and no event-study structure — it exploits no within-institution variation at all, by design. The Methods section is appropriately careful ('relationships'); the Discussion is not.
- Repeat speakers induce dependence that is never addressed: 1,875 observations come from 1,485 unique speakers, and Marian Wright Edelman alone contributes 13 of them. Because each speaker carries a single time-invariant ideology label, repeat appearances are duplicated outcome draws, not independent ones.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Rely on the overall descriptive finding — that liberal-classified speakers substantially outnumber conservative ones (1,043 vs. 310; 77%/23% of the classified) and that the liberal share rose over 1989-2024 — as the paper's firmest result. The full-period trend (0.0044/year, SE 0.0011) is a four-sigma estimate and does not depend on the contested modeling choices.
- Hold the 2011 break loosely. The post-2011 segment rests on 14 annual proportions, the difference in slopes is only about t = 2.1 once you account for both segments' standard errors, the break date was estimated from the data and then tested as if known, and the excluded 'no contribution' group grows precisely in that window. Read the post-2011 acceleration as suggestive of a real change in level of trend, not as a dated regime shift you can build a causal story on.
- Treat the public/private contrast as the paper's most durable regression result. At ME = -0.186 it is by far the largest institutional effect, it is robust across the 50% and two-thirds classification rules and the mixed-effects specification, and it is large enough that plausible clustering corrections would not eliminate it. But read it as a description of where conservative speakers appear, not as evidence about what any institution would do if its control changed.
- Discount the significance of the state-level coefficients — party control, citizen ideology, and both disinvitation counts — by an unknown but non-trivial factor for the absent clustering. These variables vary at the state-year level and their standard errors appear to be computed as if each of the 1,353 rows were independent. The citizen ideology result (0.356, p<.001) has enough margin to likely survive; the state party control result is already only p<.10 and should be treated as null-adjacent.
- Treat the disinvitation findings as the most fragile claims in the paper, and specifically do not cite them as evidence that disinvitation campaigns cause universities to change behavior. Their decay parameter was fit to the outcome, their standard errors ignore both that search and state-level clustering, and there is no year control to separate them from the secular trend — left-initiated attempts and the liberal speaker share both rise over the same period (Figure 1 vs. Figure 6). The obvious alternative reading, that left-initiated disinvitation activity is simply a marker of a liberal campus and state environment rather than an external force acting on it, is not addressed.
- Convert the proportion-variable marginal effects before quoting them. The percent-Asian ME of 1.491 is per unit of a proportion, i.e., the (off-support) 0-to-100% change; the interpretable figure is about 1.5 percentage points more likely to have a liberal speaker per 1-percentage-point increase in Asian enrollment share, or roughly 9 points across a one-SD (6.1 pp) change. The same applies to percent Hispanic (0.817) and percent occupational/professional majors (-0.230). Table 4 as printed invites a substantial misreading. Note also that the paper's own log-enrollment conversion is correct (0.047 x 0.1 = 0.47 pp per 10% enrollment increase), and that its percentages throughout are percentage points.
- Do not cite the endowment result. It is null in the primary model and appears only in an unreported specification that drops public/private control — a variable strongly correlated with endowment size and one of the largest predictors in the model. Likewise, when citing racial composition results, name Asian and Hispanic share specifically; the Black-share coefficient is a precisely uninformative zero and does not support a general 'racial diversity' claim.
- Read the selectivity results (admission rate +0.891 n.s.; yield rate -2.093, p<.05) as unresolved rather than as a finding. The two proxies point in opposite directions from what a single selectivity story would predict, both are measured in 2022 and applied back to 1989, and the paper does not reconcile them.
- Bound the generalization to the sampled institutions, not to 'U.S. universities.' Table 1 shows 32 of 52 are doctoral-granting, the first sampling stage drew from the 63 AAU members, community colleges are excluded by design, and Figure 2 shows concentration in the Northeast and on the coasts. This is a sample of relatively well-resourced four-year institutions. The 77%/23% split in particular is a property of these 52 schools and should not be read as a sector-wide baseline. The authors say as much and their caution should be carried forward.
- Before building on the covariate results, check whether they survive a year control. The paper ran year-controlled models for the decomposition but reports only the year coefficient from them. Anyone extending this work should regard the trending covariates — Asian share, Hispanic share, log enrollment, both disinvitation counts — as unverified until that specification is in hand, and should check the supplementary appendix (Tables A4, A5) for whether clustering or year controls appear there.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Design fit. The two research questions are descriptive and associational — how have speaker orientations varied over time, and how do they covary with institutional and political characteristics — and the design matches them. A pooled logit on a repeated cross-section is the right tool for a question about between-institution differences in a binary outcome, and the authors' stated reason for rejecting institution fixed effects is correct on its own terms: control, location, and selectivity are the substantive variables of interest and FE would absorb them entirely. The problem is not that the design is wrong for the questions asked; it is that the Discussion answers a third, unasked question about causal influence that the design was never built to address. Readers should keep the Methods section's framing ("relationships between the political ideologies of commencement speakers and various institutional and environmental characteristics") and mentally overwrite the Discussion's "influence," "shape," "drive," and "shifts institutional behavior" with "is associated with." This is not pedantry: the model uses no within-institution variation at all, contains no time control, and includes a regressor (state disinvitation activity) that is plausibly a proxy for the same campus political environment that produces the outcome.

Sampling and external validity. The two-stage convenience-plus-purposive design is honestly described and its main risk is handled about as well as it can be without a probability sample. The authors' key argument — that selection was on institutions, not speakers, and that they had no knowledge of speaker identities during sampling — is the right defense, and it does neutralize the most damaging form of selection bias. What it cannot neutralize is composition. Table 1 makes clear this is a sample tilted toward research universities: 32 of 52 are doctoral, and the first stage drew from the AAU membership. There are no community colleges by design, and the appendix institution list is where a reader should look to see whether minority-serving institutions, religious institutions, or regional publics are meaningfully represented (the authors themselves flag HBCUs and HSIs as future work, which suggests they are not). The practical consequence for readers is that the 77%/23% headline split is a fact about a set of mostly well-resourced four-year institutions, and quoting it as a fact about American higher education would misuse the paper. The authors say this explicitly; the abstract and title do not.

The measure. The FEC-matching work is the paper's strongest methodological asset and also its most contestable construct. On the asset side: donation-based ideology scoring is well established in the CEO literature the authors cite, the matching protocol is specific enough to audit, the 50%-versus-two-thirds robustness check is exactly the right sensitivity to run, and Table 2 lets a reader reconstruct the analytic sample exactly. On the contestable side, three things deserve a reader's attention. First, the paper contradicts itself about whether the measure is time-varying. Page 14 says the classification uses donations aggregated across 1989-2024 and "therefore does not capture potential changes in their political orientations over time," and then in the next breath claims the measure is "time-specific" and captures positioning "at the moment of selection." The operational rule described — proportion of a person's contributions going to one party — implies a single lifetime label. Readers should assume the time-invariant reading, which means that for early-period speakers the classification may be built from donations made decades after the address. Second, the classifiable share is not stable over time. The authors run the trend check for the 163 neutrality-norm occupations (Figures 3 and 4, reassuringly flat) but not for the 233 no-contribution speakers, and they state that this group grew late in the period. Since Figure 6 plots the liberal share among the classifiable, a shrinking and shifting denominator in the post-2011 window sits directly underneath the paper's most-quoted temporal finding. The direction of the bias is genuinely unknowable from the text — non-donating late-period speakers could be celebrities and athletes skewing either way — so this is a reason for width in one's uncertainty rather than a directional correction. Third, elected officials are coded by party registration while everyone else is coded by donation behavior, mixing two constructs under one label; this is probably innocuous but is worth knowing.

Estimation. The most consequential technical gap is the absence of any clustering. The paper never uses the word, and the Table 4 note documents only the imputation and marginal-effects commands. With 52 institutions contributing an average of 26 observations each, and with four of the seventeen regressors literally constant within institution, the standard errors on those four are computed against a nominal N of 1,353 when the information content is closer to 52. The state-level variables are in the same position with respect to states. The authors do offer an implicit defense: the likelihood-ratio test against the mixed-effects model returns 1.71 with p > .05, which they read as showing that institution-level dependence is negligible. That is a real piece of evidence and it should not be dismissed, but it carries less weight than it appears to. The test is on a variance parameter at the boundary of the parameter space, so its null distribution is a mixture rather than the chi-square being used; a failure to reject a random-intercept variance does not license unclustered standard errors in general; and a random intercept addresses institution-level residual correlation, not the serial correlation in slowly-moving state political variables that drives the Moulton problem. My reading is that the public/private effect (-0.186) is large enough to survive any plausible correction, while the results sitting at p < .05 with t-statistics between 2 and 2.6 — location, yield rate, occupational majors, and both disinvitation terms — are the ones a correction could plausibly move to insignificance.

The missing year control is the second structural issue and it interacts badly with the first. Table 4 has no time variable. Over 1989-2024 the outcome trends up, and so do percent Hispanic students, percent Asian students, log enrollment, and both disinvitation counts — all for reasons exogenous to commencement. A pooled cross-section with no time control cannot distinguish a genuine association from co-trending. The authors clearly estimated year-controlled versions, because the decomposition requires them, but they report only the year marginal effect from those runs and never the covariate estimates. This is the single most useful thing a reader would want and it is not in the paper. It also undercuts the decomposition's own interpretation: the finding that adding covariates shrinks the year effect from 0.0044 to a non-significant 0.0017 is arithmetically equivalent to saying the covariates are collinear with time, which is guaranteed by construction for the trending ones. Calling that "our model accounts for about 62% of the observed time trend," and then in the Discussion "organizational and environmental factors drive a substantial share of the change," reads mechanism into what is a statement about shared trends.

Tuning parameters and inference. Two parameters in this paper were chosen by looking at the outcome and then tested as if they had been fixed in advance. The decay factor is the clearer case: the authors write that they "tested various decay factors to assess how well this variable predicted commencement speakers' political ideologies" and that the analysis "pointed to a decay factor of ~0.8." That is fitting a functional-form parameter to the dependent variable and then reporting nominal p-values for the coefficient it produces. Those coefficients (0.129 and -0.183) have t-statistics of roughly 2.5 and 2.1 before any adjustment for either the search or clustering, so they have very little room. The break point is the same problem in a different form: it is "estimated through the model-fitting process," which makes the subsequent t-test on the post-2011 slope non-standard. Independently, the piecewise regression is unweighted OLS on 36 annual proportions whose denominators vary considerably (some pandemic years have few observations), so the assumption of homoskedastic year-level errors is not met either. Differencing the two segment slopes by hand gives 0.0111 with a standard error near 0.0052 — about t = 2.1, before any adjustment for the estimated break. The break is real enough to describe; it is not solid enough to build a dating argument on.

The imputation. Twenty imputations with mi estimate and mimrgns is the correct machinery, and it means the reported standard errors do propagate imputation uncertainty rather than treating imputed values as data. What is missing is any account of the imputation model or the missingness pattern. Twenty percent of citizen ideology values are missing, and the Berry et al. series has known endpoint coverage limitations, which makes it likely the missingness clusters in particular years rather than scattering at random across the panel. If those years fall late in the period, then a key trending regressor is being partly reconstructed from other trending regressors during exactly the window where the outcome trend accelerates, and both the citizen ideology coefficient and the decomposition inherit that. A complete-case comparison would settle it in one line and is not offered.

Reading Table 4 correctly. The marginal effects on proportion-scaled variables are reported per unit of the proportion, meaning a hypothetical 0-to-100% change. The percent-Asian ME of 1.491 therefore does not mean a 149-percentage-point change in probability; it means roughly 1.5 percentage points per 1-percentage-point increase in Asian enrollment share, or about 9 points across one standard deviation (6.1 points) of that variable. Percent Hispanic (0.817) and percent occupational/professional majors (-0.230) need the same treatment. The paper's narration does not perform this conversion for the racial composition variables, though it does get the enrollment conversion right (0.047 per unit of log enrollment times 0.0953 for a 10% increase gives about 0.45 points, close to the 0.47 quoted). Note also that the paper's "18.6%" for public institutions and "5.5%" for urban location are percentage points, not percentages.

What is load-bearing and what is not. Firm: the overall composition of speakers in this sample, the full-period upward trend in the liberal share, and the public/private gap. These rest on the data collection rather than on modeling choices, replicate across the 50% and two-thirds rules and across the pooled and mixed-effects specifications, and are large relative to any plausible standard-error correction. Moderately supported: citizen ideology, percent occupational/professional majors, and log enrollment — directionally plausible, consistent with theory, but untested against year controls and computed with standard errors that are probably too small. Fragile: the disinvitation results, the yield-rate result, the state party control result (already only p < .10), and the endowment claim, which is null in the primary model and appears significant only in an unreported specification that drops public/private control. Not supported: any causal reading of disinvitation pressure on institutional behavior, the framing that speaker selection is demonstrably "permeable to organized external pressure," and the abstract's implication that racial diversity broadly predicts liberal speakers when the Black-share coefficient is 0.215 with a standard error of 1.826.

On calibration. I want to be clear that the gaps above are mostly gaps in inferential execution and reporting, not in the underlying evidence. This paper does something no one else has done and does the hard part — building the dataset — carefully and transparently. An adequate rating reflects a strong empirical foundation with a regression layer that is under-documented on clustering, under-specified on time, and over-read in the Discussion. Nothing I have identified overturns the paper's central descriptive contribution.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (low confidence)

The paper is well read in the sociology of campus speech and unusually attentive to comparative (British no-platforming) work, and it is honest in the abstract about the coarseness of its ideology measure. But it is thinly positioned in the two literatures its own design depends on most — campaign-finance-based ideology measurement (Bonica's DIME/CFscores and its elite-scoring applications) and the state-politics debate over the Berry et al. citizen ideology series — and it invokes organizational theory more as framing vocabulary than as a source of testable propositions, omitting the single most apposite citation (Meyer & Rowan 1977 on ceremony) for a paper about ceremonial symbolic acts. Readers should treat the substantive campus-speech coverage as trustworthy and the methodological positioning as incomplete.

**Strengths:**

- Current and accurate coverage of the core campus-speech literature it does engage: Kidder & Binder (2021), Binder & Wood (2012), Boch (2022), Garces et al. (2021), Perrin et al. (2025), Berrey et al. (2024), Andrews & Ngo (2026), and the faculty-composition strand (Gross 2013; Langbert & Stevens 2022; Havey & Her 2025; Magness & Waugh 2022). The reference list runs current through 2026, which is rare and valuable in a field where campus-speech scholarship dates quickly.
- The comparative move to Smith (2020, 2024) on British no-platforming is a genuine and uncommon strength. Most U.S. higher-education work on campus speech is hermetically domestic; grounding platform allocation in the longer institutional history of student-union no-platforming gives the concept a lineage rather than inventing it fresh, and the discussion's call for U.K. comparative work follows naturally from it.
- The paper is candid about the limits of its liberal/conservative dichotomy, and the 'Conceptualizing Political Orientation' section does real work — Bobbio (1996) on the historical contingency of left/right and Grossmann & Hopkins (2016) on asymmetric coalitional structure are both apt, correctly used, and more careful than most education-research treatments of ideology.
- The treatment of conservative critiques of the academy (Buckley 1951; Bloom 1987; D'Souza 1991; Kors & Silverglate 1999; Douthat 2015; French 2016) is even-handed in register: they are cited as characterizing a durable discourse and a source of political pressure, not endorsed as findings, and the paper pairs them with the empirical literature that complicates them (Gross 2013; Woessner & Kelly-Woessner 2020). The framing is descriptive rather than polemical in either direction.
- The paper explicitly names and addresses a rival explanation — publicity/prestige — rather than ignoring it, and cites the reputational-competition literature (Clark 1983; Sauder 2008) that motivates it.

**Weaknesses:**

- The campaign-finance-as-ideology literature is essentially absent. The paper's measure — FEC contributions collapsed to a binary by majority rule — cites only the corporate-governance applications (Christensen et al. 2015; Cohen et al. 2019; Hutton et al. 2014) and never engages Adam Bonica's DIME/CFscore framework, which is the standard validated ideal-point scaling built from exactly this FEC universe, is continuous rather than binary, is estimated by election cycle rather than pooled, and has been used to score precisely this kind of elite population (law professors, physicians, lawyers, corporate executives). A reader cannot tell from this paper that a more established alternative existed and was not used.
- A specific, checkable overstatement follows from that gap. The paper excludes 163 judges, journalists, clergy, and military officers on the grounds that 'there is no systematic or reliable strategy' for inferring their political leanings. For judges this is not accurate: Bonica & Sen's campaign-finance-based judicial ideology scores and the earlier Judicial Common Space (Epstein et al.) are exactly such strategies and are widely used in political science and law. The exclusion may still be defensible on other grounds, but the stated justification misdescribes the state of the literature.
- The novelty claim — 'the first systematic longitudinal evidence of how universities allocate highly visible speaking platforms' — is stated more strongly than the paper's engagement with antecedents supports. Rutherford (2004), which the paper itself cites, is a longitudinal analysis of twentieth-century commencement addresses (content rather than speaker ideology, but longitudinal and on the same ceremony). Advocacy and think-tank organizations, most visibly Young America's Foundation, have published recurring tallies of commencement speaker partisanship at leading institutions for well over a decade, and Campus Reform and ACTA have produced related counts; these are not peer-reviewed and are methodologically weaker, but they are the direct predecessors of the paper's headline descriptive finding and go unmentioned. The defensible claim is narrower — the first peer-reviewed, multi-institution, covariate-adjusted longitudinal analysis — and the paper does not draw that line.
- Berry et al. (2007) is cited for citizen ideology with no acknowledgment of the sustained methodological debate over that series, most pointedly the Enns & Koch exchange in State Politics & Policy Quarterly over whether the Berry measures are comparable across years. The paper uses citizen ideology as a time-varying covariate across 35 years and reports it as one of its strongest findings, so the over-time comparability question is directly load-bearing. Alternative dynamic state-opinion measures (Tausanovitch & Warshaw; Caughey & Warshaw) are not mentioned.
- Organizational theory is invoked rather than deployed. Pfeffer & Salancik (1978), DiMaggio & Powell (1983), Suchman (1995), Scott (1995), and Ray (2019) each appear as one-line warrants for general propositions; none generates a differentiated prediction. DiMaggio & Powell's coercive/mimetic/normative distinction is never applied, though mimetic isomorphism implies a testable convergence-across-peers hypothesis. Suchman's pragmatic/moral/cognitive typology is named but not used to separate mechanisms. Resource dependence is not operationalized through Pfeffer & Salancik's own dimensions (concentration, munificence, interconnectedness), and the revenue-share results that would bear on it are null and left largely uninterpreted.
- Two canonical citations that the argument almost requires are missing. Meyer & Rowan (1977) on formal structure as myth and ceremony is the foundational statement of the paper's own thesis — that ceremonial practice manages legitimacy — and does not appear. Oliver (1991) on strategic responses to institutional processes is the standard citation for the paper's concluding claim that universities are 'strategic organizations navigating legitimacy under varying political conditions,' and is likewise absent. Bromley & Powell on decoupling and Elsbach's work on impression management after controversy would also have sharpened the mechanism.
- The higher-education-policy literature on state political environments is not cited at all, despite being the closest disciplinary home for the paper's state-level covariates. The tradition running through McLendon, Hearn, Tandberg, and Doyle on how partisan control and state political context shape institutional and system behavior is the obvious antecedent for the paper's second research question, and the authors' own prior campus-carry work sits squarely within it.
- The rebuttal to the publicity explanation does not follow. The paper argues that if publicity drove selection, 'we would expect similar patterns of speaker orientation across organizational contexts.' That holds only if the pool of prominent, available, willing speakers is identical across institutions — which is implausible, since alumni networks, region, sector ties, and institutional prestige all shape who can plausibly be landed. A supply-side account (the professional composition of the American public-figure elite, and its documented partisan sorting by occupation) predicts much of the same cross-sectional variation the paper reads as organizational logic, and no literature bearing on elite composition is engaged.
- A related supply-side confound with the headline temporal finding goes unaddressed and uncited: sitting presidents, cabinet officials, and their allies are heavily represented on the commencement circuit, so the partisan composition of the federal executive mechanically shifts the available pool. The 2011 break point sits inside a long stretch of Democratic executive incumbency. No literature on political-office-holding and public appearance is engaged.
- The post-structural gesture (Kitching et al. 2025; Youdell 2010) occupies a single sentence and is immediately set aside as directing attention 'toward individual-level dynamics and discursive processes.' This is a compressed and arguably unfair characterization of a tradition centrally concerned with institutional governance of speech, and it reads as a citation of acknowledgment rather than engagement.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Before repeating this paper's measurement approach, read Bonica's DIME/CFscore papers (Bonica 2014, American Journal of Political Science, 'Mapping the Ideological Marketplace') and the elite-scoring applications built on it — Bonica, Chilton, Rozema & Sen on the legal academy; Bonica, Rosenthal & Rothman on physicians; Bonica & Sen on lawyers and judges. That literature is the real methodological antecedent for scoring an elite population by FEC donations, and it makes clear that this paper's binary, pooled-over-35-years classification is a design choice with continuous, cycle-specific alternatives, not a necessity.
- Treat the sentence claiming 'no systematic or reliable strategy' exists for inferring the ideology of judges and journalists as inaccurate as written, and do not cite the paper for that proposition. Campaign-finance-based judicial ideology measures and the Judicial Common Space are well established. This does not invalidate the exclusion decision, but the stated rationale should not be repeated.
- Read the 'first systematic longitudinal evidence' claim narrowly. Cite this paper for the first peer-reviewed multi-institution longitudinal analysis of commencement speaker partisanship with institutional and state-political covariates — a real contribution. Do not cite it for the descriptive finding that liberal speakers predominate at selective institutions, which advocacy tallies (Young America's Foundation and others) have reported for more than a decade and which this paper neither cites nor engages. Rutherford (2004), cited in the paper, remains the antecedent for longitudinal analysis of commencement as a genre.
- Before relying on the citizen-ideology result, consult the Enns & Koch / Berry et al. exchange in State Politics & Policy Quarterly on whether the Berry citizen ideology series supports over-time comparisons, and consider Tausanovitch & Warshaw or Caughey & Warshaw as alternative dynamic state-opinion measures. This debate is directly relevant to a 35-year panel and the paper does not flag it.
- For the theoretical apparatus, go to the sources rather than the paper's summaries. Meyer & Rowan (1977) is the missing foundation for the ceremony-as-legitimacy argument; Oliver (1991) supplies the typology of strategic organizational responses to institutional pressure that the discussion's conclusion presupposes; Espeland & Sauder (2007) on rankings reactivity is the developed version of the reputational-environment argument that Sauder (2008) only gestures at here. Readers wanting to build on this paper theoretically should treat its organizational-theory section as an entry point, not a synthesis.
- Situate the state-politics findings in the higher-education-policy literature the paper omits — McLendon, Hearn, Tandberg, and Doyle on partisan control, state political context, and postsecondary policy adoption, and the authors' own Johnson & Zhang (2020) campus-carry study. Read this way, the paper is a new outcome variable within an established research program on state political environments and institutional behavior, which is a more accurate placement than the paper's own 'new organizational lens' framing.
- Hold the publicity and supply-side explanations open. The paper's rebuttal to the publicity account rests on an assumption of a common speaker pool across institutions that it does not defend and no cited literature supports. Given documented partisan sorting by occupation among political donors, an account in which the changing composition of prominent public figures drives much of both the temporal trend and the cross-sectional variation remains live. The paper's own discussion concedes this possibility for the parallel rise in women and non-White speakers but does not extend the concession to its main finding.
- Verify two descriptive characterizations before repeating them. First, the paper describes Kidder & Binder (2021) as drawing on interviews with student activists 'at four flagship universities'; the related Binder & Wood (2012) book studies two pseudonymized campuses, so the sample description is worth checking against the source. Second, Stevens, Armstrong & Arum (2008) is cited twice for claims about commencement ritual and about speaker prominence as prestige and publicity; it is a broad review essay in the sociology of higher education, not an empirical source on commencement speakers, and should not be cited as evidence for either claim.
- Note an internal inconsistency in how the ideology measure is described. The Variables section states that classification is based on donations aggregated across 1989–2024 and 'therefore does not capture potential changes in [speakers'] political orientations over time,' and then, one sentence later, that 'because we measure political orientation using time-specific campaign contributions, our operationalization captures speakers' positioning relative to the political landscape at the moment of selection.' These cannot both be true. Readers assessing the temporal findings should assume the former — a static, pooled classification — which is the more conservative and, on the paper's own description of the matching procedure, the more likely reading.
- Readers approaching this paper for evidence about ideological bias in higher education should note that it deliberately declines to adjudicate that question. It documents a strong and growing liberal skew among identifiable speakers (77% liberal under the majority rule) and then pivots to organizational framing rather than engaging the Buckley–Bloom–D'Souza critiques it cites in the introduction. That is a defensible scope decision, not a flaw, but the paper is not the empirical resolution of those debates and should not be cited as such.
- Companion readings that supply context the paper omits: Meyer & Rowan (1977) and Oliver (1991) for the organizational mechanism; Bonica (2014) for ideology measurement; Ray (2019) read directly rather than through the paper's future-directions gesture, given that racial composition does empirical work in the models while racialized-organization theory is deferred to the conclusion; and Pitkin's distinction between descriptive and symbolic representation, which is the concept the paper needs where it instead reaches for Mansbridge (1999) on descriptive representation by legislators.

**Detailed Commentary:**

The scholarly positioning of this paper divides cleanly into a domain literature it knows well and two methodological literatures it does not engage. The domain coverage is genuinely competent. The introduction's two-strand map of campus-speech research — an individual-attitudes strand (Binder & Wood 2012; Gross 2013; Woessner & Kelly-Woessner 2020) and a controversy/dilemma strand (Boch 2022; Kidder & Binder 2021) — is a fair first-order description, the sources are correctly identified, and the recency of the reference list (Andrews & Ngo 2026; Perrin et al. 2025; Schachle-Gordon et al. 2025; Havey & Her 2025) is unusual and useful. The Smith (2020, 2024) material on British no-platforming is the best-integrated body of prior work in the paper, and it does real conceptual work rather than serving as decoration.

The framing that organizes the whole paper — prior work studies 'individual perceptions, attitudes, and episodic conflicts,' whereas this paper studies organizational practice — is defensible in broad outline but overdrawn in a way readers should notice. The paper's own citations partly contradict it. Garces et al. (2021) on 'repressive legalism' is precisely a study of organizational response to speech conflict, analyzing how administrators handle competing pressures; the paper cites it accurately but files it under the conflict strand it is arguing past. Berrey et al. (2024) examines university and police responses to protest — again organizational behavior. And in the reverse direction, Boch (2022) is placed in the controversy/organizational-dilemma strand when it is closer to a study of tolerance and attitudes toward extreme speakers. The sorting is a little convenient. The stronger and more accurate version of the paper's claim is narrower: prior organizational work on campus speech has been reactive and case-based, studying how institutions respond after a controversy erupts, whereas this paper studies a routine, recurring, universal decision observed for every institution-year regardless of whether controversy occurred. That framing survives scrutiny; the broader one does not.

The more consequential problem is the paper's positioning relative to the literature on measuring elite ideology from campaign finance. The entire empirical apparatus rests on classifying 1,353 speakers by the partisan direction of their FEC contributions, and the only citations offered are three corporate-governance papers that used a similar heuristic for CEOs (Christensen et al. 2015; Cohen et al. 2019; Hutton et al. 2014). Adam Bonica's DIME project — which scales the near-universe of federal contributors 1979 onward into continuous, cycle-specific ideal points, and which has been used to score exactly this sort of professional elite (law faculty, physicians, lawyers, executives) — is nowhere in the paper. This matters for readers in three ways. First, it makes the novelty claim harder to calibrate: 'first systematic longitudinal evidence' reads differently once one knows that donation-based ideological scoring of institutional elites is an established genre with its own methodological standards. Second, the paper's binary, majority-rule classification pooled over the full 35 years is a design choice with a well-validated alternative, and readers evaluating the measurement should know a continuous, time-varying option existed. Third, and most concretely, the paper's rationale for dropping 163 speakers in 'neutral' professions asserts that no systematic strategy exists for inferring the ideology of judges and journalists — a claim that is simply not true for judges, where campaign-finance-derived scores and the Judicial Common Space are standard tools. Any reader tempted to repeat that sentence should not.

The same pattern recurs with the state-politics covariate. Berry, Ringquist, Fording & Hanson (2007) is the right citation for state citizen ideology, but the paper presents it as a settled instrument rather than as a measure with a live methodological controversy attached — specifically over whether the series can be compared across years, which is exactly how this paper uses it across a 35-year window, and which bears directly on one of the two findings the abstract foregrounds. The relevant exchange appeared in State Politics & Policy Quarterly and is not obscure. Nor does the paper mention the newer dynamic state-opinion measures that were developed partly in response to those concerns. Combined with the absence of the higher-education-policy tradition on state political environments (McLendon, Hearn, Tandberg, Doyle), the state-level half of the analysis is the most thinly positioned part of the paper, which is unfortunate because it is also the part that produces the results the discussion treats as most novel.

On organizational theory, the paper cites the right names and does comparatively little with them. Pfeffer & Salancik, DiMaggio & Powell, Suchman, Scott, Tierney, and Ray each supply a general warrant; none generates a prediction that distinguishes this paper's hypotheses from what a reader would guess without theory. Public institutions face state pressure, elite private ones do not — this is a plausible reading of resource dependence, but it is also common sense, and Pfeffer & Salancik's actual analytic machinery goes unused. DiMaggio & Powell's isomorphism typology would imply a testable convergence hypothesis across peer institutions; it is not tested. Suchman's three legitimacy types are invoked as one construct. Ray (2019) is the most awkward case: racial composition of the student body is a substantively important covariate in the models — the Asian and Hispanic enrollment coefficients are among the largest — yet racialized organization theory is introduced in one paragraph as a 'complementary lens' and then deferred to future research, with the actual interpretive work done by Mansbridge (1999) on descriptive representation, imported from political theory and applied by analogy to a context Mansbridge was not writing about. The absence of Meyer & Rowan (1977) is the sharpest omission. A paper arguing that a ceremonial practice functions to manage organizational legitimacy is restating, in a new domain, the central claim of the founding paper on formal structure as myth and ceremony. Its absence, alongside Oliver (1991) on strategic responses — which is what the discussion's closing characterization of universities as strategic legitimacy-navigating organizations actually describes — leaves the theoretical framing looking assembled from higher-education-adjacent citations rather than from the organizational literature's own spine.

On balance and even-handedness, the treatment of conservative critique is defensible. Buckley, Bloom, D'Souza, Kors & Silverglate, Douthat, and French are cited as expressions of a durable political discourse and as evidence that universities face scrutiny — which is what they are — rather than as findings, and Gross (2013) and Woessner & Kelly-Woessner (2020) supply empirical counterweight. What is missing is not balance but resolution. The paper reports that 77 percent of classifiable speakers are liberal and that the share is rising, a finding directly relevant to the claims those critics make, and then declines to say anything about whether it supports or complicates them, redirecting to organizational variation. That is a legitimate scope choice; readers should simply be clear that the paper is not the empirical adjudication of the bias debate that its descriptive statistics might seem to promise.

Finally, the engagement with conflicting evidence is present but weak at the decisive point. The paper does confront the publicity/prestige alternative, which is more than many papers would do. But the rebuttal — that publicity would predict uniform speaker orientation across contexts — assumes a common speaker pool, and neither cites nor engages any literature on who prominent American public figures are, how their donation behavior sorts by profession, or how that composition has shifted over 35 years. The paper itself half-concedes the point in its discussion of the parallel rise in women and non-White speakers, listing 'the changing composition of prominent public figures across sectors' as an open question, but does not extend that concession to its main result. A closely related supply-side confound goes unmentioned entirely: sitting officeholders and their allies are heavily represented at commencements, so the partisan composition of the federal executive shifts the available pool, and the paper's 2011 break point falls within an extended period of Democratic incumbency. Neither the paper's covariates nor its literature engage this.

A note on the limits of my own assessment. I am confident about the organizational-theory canon, about the campaign-finance ideology literature and its elite-scoring applications, and about the existence of the state citizen-ideology measurement debate. I am less certain about the precise form and dating of the gray-literature commencement-speaker tallies I reference — I believe Young America's Foundation has published such counts annually for a decade or more, but readers should verify rather than take my characterization on faith. I am also uncertain whether a peer-reviewed empirical literature on honorary-degree conferral exists in a form that would qualify as a direct antecedent here; if it does, it would further narrow the novelty claim. And the specific detail I flag in the paper's description of Kidder & Binder's sample is a flag for verification, not an assertion of error.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper is clearly written at the sentence level, conventionally organized, and unusually candid in its Methods about sampling and measurement choices, so a reader can generally follow what was done. But several fidelity lapses survived production: a headline claim about endowments that the paper's only reported regression table contradicts, a self-contradictory description of the central political-orientation measure, a Results paragraph that describes content its own figure excludes, and causal verbs in the abstract and discussion that no part of the design supports. Readers should treat Table 4 and the Figure 6 note as the authoritative record and verify prose claims against them before quoting.

**Strengths:**

- The Methods section is exceptionally transparent about the awkward parts of the design: the two-stage convenience-plus-purposive sampling is described honestly (including the AAU starting point and the tilt toward well-resourced institutions), the FEC matching procedure is spelled out, and each excluded category of speaker (163 'unique occupations,' 91 foreign nationals, 233 with no records, 35 unclear) is named, counted, and justified rather than buried.
- Table 2 is fully self-contained and arithmetically clean: the 50% and two-thirds columns each sum exactly to 1,875 and to 100.00%, the note defines both rules, and a reader can reconstruct the analytic sample (1,043 + 310 = 1,353) directly from it without trusting the prose.
- Table 4 is internally coherent to an unusual degree. Every reported marginal effect is the logit coefficient times a constant 0.1525-0.1536, so a reader can verify each cell independently; significance stars are reported at four thresholds including a distinct '+' for p < .10 rather than collapsing everything into one asterisk.
- Figure 6's note is a model of exhibit self-containment: it gives the pooled slope (0.0044, SE 0.0011), both piecewise slopes (0.0010, SE 0.0022 before 2011; 0.0121, SE 0.0047 after), and the estimated break point, so a reader can assess the paper's central temporal claim from the note alone.
- The 'Conceptualizing Political Orientation' subsection does real work most quantitative papers skip, explicitly bounding the liberal/conservative labels to contemporary U.S. partisan alignment and warning against reading them as institutional ideology.
- The Discussion pre-empts the most obvious alternative explanation (publicity/prestige) directly rather than ignoring it, and the argument it offers against it -- that a pure publicity story predicts uniform patterns across organizational contexts -- is the right shape of argument even if the underlying evidence is correlational.

**Weaknesses:**

- The endowment claim is not supported by any reported result. Table 4 shows the endowment revenue ratio at 0.034 (SE 0.026), ME 0.005 (SE 0.004) -- comfortably insignificant. The Results text concedes 'Financial factors appear to have limited influence,' then adds that 'in a separate model excluding public/private control ... the endowment size is positively and significantly related to having liberal speakers.' That model appears nowhere -- not in Table 4, not among the listed appendix tables (A4 is the two-thirds rule, A5 the mixed-effects model). Yet the claim is promoted to the Introduction ('liberal speakers are more prevalent at larger institutions with more racially diverse student bodies and larger endowments') and stated flatly in the Discussion ('universities with more racially diverse student bodies and larger endowments tend toward liberal speakers'). A reader who skips the Results will carry away a finding that the paper's own table contradicts, sourced to a specification that drops the single strongest predictor in the model (public control, ME -0.186).
- The description of the political-orientation measure contradicts itself in consecutive sentences. Page 14 says classification 'is based on each speaker's aggregated political donations between 1989 and 2024 and therefore does not capture potential changes in their political orientations over time.' The very next sentence begins 'Furthermore, because we measure political orientation using time-specific campaign contributions, our operationalization captures speakers' positioning relative to the political landscape at the moment of selection.' These cannot both be true, and the connective 'Furthermore' presents them as additive when they are opposed. This is load-bearing, not cosmetic: under the aggregated reading, a 1992 speaker's label may rest on donations made in 2015, which would make Figure 6's time trend partly an artifact of donation histories rather than of changing invitation behavior. The text gives readers no way to determine which was actually done.
- 'Racially diverse student bodies' overstates the race results. Percent Black is 0.215 with SE 1.826 -- a coefficient dwarfed by its own standard error, and the one group the Theoretical Foundation builds its argument around (Black students at predominantly White institutions, citing Hope et al. and Moore & Bell). Percent Hispanic is significant only at p < .10. Only percent Asian clears p < .05. The Results text says 'particularly Hispanic and Asian' without flagging the Hispanic result's marginal status; the abstract omits race entirely (correctly), but the Introduction and Discussion assert the diversity claim without qualification.
- The disinvitation results rest on a tuning parameter chosen against the outcome, and the prose never says so. The Methods report that 'we tested various decay factors to assess how well this variable predicted commencement speakers' political ideologies. Our analysis pointed to a decay factor of ~0.8.' The resulting p < .05 coefficients in Table 4 are therefore conditioned on a search over decay specifications, and their nominal significance is not what it appears. The Discussion nonetheless escalates to causal language: 'The evidence that disinvitation efforts influence institutional behavior suggests that speaker selection is more permeable to organized external pressure than is often acknowledged.' Nothing in a pooled logistic regression on state-year counts licenses 'influence' or 'permeable.'
- The Figure 5 paragraph describes content the figure explicitly excludes. The opening sentence says Figure 5 focuses 'only the proportion of liberal and conversative speakers and excluding those whose political orientations could not be identified.' Three sentences later: 'The number of speakers with no political contributions also increased late in the study period. The number of foreign contributors and speakers with unique occupations or unclear classifications remained relatively stable.' Those are counts of the excluded categories -- readable from Figure 3, not Figure 5. The paragraph conflates three exhibits and the reader must go hunting.
- The post-2011 acceleration is attributed to a left/right split that the cited figure does not show. 'This acceleration appears to align with an increase in speech disinvitation attempts from the left during the same period, as depicted in Figure 1.' Figure 1's caption is simply 'Number of campus speech disinvitation attempts over time,' with a FIRE source note and no indication of any ideological decomposition. The reader cannot verify the claim from the exhibit it points to.
- The abstract's headline N overstates the analytic sample by 39%. It reports analyzing 'the political orientations of 1,875 commencement speakers,' but political orientation was determined for only 1,353; Table 4's N is 1,353, and 522 observations (27.8%) are excluded. The abstract also does not signal that the unit is speaker-institution-year rather than speaker (there are 1,485 unique individuals; Marian Wright Edelman is counted 13 times), nor that the 52 institutions are a convenience/purposive sample skewed toward AAU members and the coasts. The Methods are candid about all three; the abstract, which many readers will not read past, is not.
- The abstract and Discussion use causal verbs throughout -- speaker selection is 'shaped by' institutional characteristics, external environments 'shape speaker selection,' disinvitation efforts 'influence institutional behavior,' the direction of disinvitation campaigns 'shifts institutional behavior' -- for a pooled cross-sectional logistic regression with no identification strategy. There is no consolidated Limitations section anywhere, and the absence of causal identification is never stated in any form.
- Table 4's note discloses that 'Multiple imputation was used to address missing data for "citizen ideology" in about 20% of cases.' This appears nowhere in the Methods text. Citizen ideology is the strongest environmental result in the paper (p < .001) and features in the abstract; a fifth of it being imputed, and why (the Berry et al. series does not cover the full 1989-2024 window), belongs in the body, not a table note.
- The Table 4 marginal effects are uninterpretable as stated for the continuous proportion variables. The paper defines them as 'the change in the probability of a speaker being liberal for each one-unit change in the independent variable,' but percent Asian has ME = 1.491 and percent Hispanic 0.817 -- probability changes exceeding 1 and approaching it, because a 'one-unit change' means going from 0% to 100% Asian enrollment (the variable's mean is 0.073). These are local linear approximations extrapolated absurdly far. The text quietly declines to quote either number, which spares the reader the nonsense but also leaves the table's largest-looking effects unexplained.
- The enrollment marginal effect is translated slightly wrong and in ambiguous units. 'For every 10% increase in total enrollment, the likelihood of inviting a conservative speaker decreases by 0.47%.' The ME is 0.047 per log unit, and a 10% enrollment increase is ln(1.1) = 0.0953 log units, so the correct figure is 0.45 percentage points; the authors used 0.1. More consequentially, '%' throughout the Results denotes percentage points (18.6% for public control, 5.5% for urban location), which a reader can easily misread as a relative change -- and it matters, because an 18.6 percentage-point shift against a 23% conservative base rate is far larger than '18.6%' sounds.
- The 2011 break point is data-selected and then treated as established. The Methods say the 'reflection point' was estimated 'through the model-fitting process' after 'observing a potential shift in temporal patterns around 2010'; the text then says 'The analysis confirmed a break point between 2010 and 2011.' No test of whether the two segment slopes differ is reported (by hand: 0.0121 vs 0.0010, t ~ 2.14, borderline), and no adjustment is made for the breakpoint having been chosen from the data. The abstract's 'particularly since 2011' rests on this. The narrower text also leaves 2010 itself unassigned, saying 'Prior to 2010' in one sentence and 'from 2011 onward' in the next.
- Production errors survived that a careful reader will notice and that undermine confidence in the numbers: 'likelihood ration = 1.71' (a garbled likelihood-ratio statistic, in the sentence that justifies the paper's choice of primary specification); 'conversative speakers'; 'more liberal learnings of the state's general population'; 'focusing only the proportion' (missing 'on'); 'log odds ratio (0.399)' for what is a log-odds coefficient, not an odds ratio; 'National State Council of Legislatures' where the paper elsewhere correctly cites the National Conference of State Legislatures; and 'Kors & Silvergate, 1999' in text against 'Silverglate' in the reference list.
- The theoretical front matter is disproportionate. Background, Theoretical Foundation, and Conceptualizing Political Orientation run from roughly page 4 to page 10 -- about a third of the article -- before any data appear, and much of it restates the same claim (speaker selection is symbolic platform allocation shaped by internal culture and external environment) in successive paraphrases. The Results, which carry all the empirical content, occupy roughly three pages. The Discussion is longer than the Results, and a substantial share of it is future-research agenda-setting (four numbered directions) rather than interpretation of what was found.
- The rise in 'no contribution' speakers late in the period is mentioned once, in a subordinate clause of the Figure 5 paragraph, and never revisited -- even though every trend analysis conditions on speakers whose orientation could be classified. If the classifiable share is shifting compositionally over time, Figure 6's post-2011 rise is partly about who drops out of the denominator. The prose does not raise this, and readers must notice it themselves.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read Table 4 and the Figure 6 note before reading the Discussion, and treat them as the paper's factual record. Every quantitative claim worth citing is in those two places; the Discussion's summary of them is looser than they are.
- Do not cite this paper for a relationship between endowment size and liberal speakers. Table 4's endowment coefficient (0.034, SE 0.026) is null. The significant result quoted in the Introduction and Discussion comes from an unreported model that drops public/private control -- the strongest predictor in the model -- and that specification appears in no table or appendix.
