- If your use of the paper depends on the time trend, read the two contradictory sentences on p. 14 about the orientation measure carefully and treat the question as unresolved. Whether speakers were classified from donations aggregated across the whole 1989-2024 window or from contemporaneous donations changes what Figure 6 means. The paper asserts both.
- When citing sample size, use 1,353 (the estimation sample, given in Table 4's title), not the abstract's 1,875. And describe the unit as speaker-institution-year observations across 52 institutions, not as 1,875 speakers -- there are 1,485 unique individuals, some appearing more than a dozen times.
- Quote the disinvitation findings only with the caveat that the decay factor (~0.8) applied to the disinvitation variable was selected by testing 'how well this variable predicted' the outcome. The reported p < .05 does not account for that search. The Discussion's language about institutions being 'permeable to organized external pressure' goes well past what the estimate supports.
- Treat the state-partisan-control result as suggestive, not established: the coefficient is 0.399 at p < .10, which the Results text calls 'significant' and the abstract elevates to state government control shaping speaker selection.
- Do not quote the percent-Asian (1.491) or percent-Hispanic (0.817) marginal effects as probability changes. All Table 4 marginal effects are the logit coefficient times a constant 0.153, so they carry no information beyond the coefficients, and for variables scaled 0-1 they represent an extrapolation from 0% to 100% enrollment share. Percent Black (0.215, SE 1.826) is a precise null -- worth noting given the paper's theoretical framing around Black students at predominantly White institutions.
- Read Table 4's note, not just the table. It discloses that citizen ideology -- the strongest environmental predictor and an abstract-level claim -- was multiply imputed in about 20% of cases. That disclosure appears nowhere in the Methods text.
- The Sample and Variables subsections (pp. 10-17) are the paper's most trustworthy prose and should not be skipped by anyone assessing generalizability; they contain the sampling caveats, the exclusion counts, and the FEC matching procedure. There is no separate Limitations section, so this is where the limitations live.
- The Background and Theoretical Foundation sections (pp. 4-10) can be skimmed for the two organizing perspectives -- organizational culture (internal characteristics) and institutional/resource dependency (external environments) -- which are restated compactly in the Introduction. Little in these pages constrains the empirical analysis.
- Figures 3, 4, and 5 are descriptive and can be skimmed, but note that the paragraph nominally describing Figure 5 actually makes claims about excluded-category counts that only Figure 3 displays. Figure 1 shows total disinvitation attempts nationally; the Results paragraph that cites it for a specifically left-initiated increase is asserting something the figure does not show.
- Read the paper's verbs skeptically. 'Shape,' 'influence,' 'drive,' and 'accounts for' appear throughout the abstract and Discussion for what is a pooled logistic regression with no identification strategy and no discussion of confounding. The '~62% of the observed time trend' figure is attenuation of a year coefficient (0.0044 to 0.0017) when covariates are added, not explained variance, and no test of the difference is reported.

**Detailed Commentary:**

This is competent, readable academic prose with a conventional and navigable structure, published in a top-tier journal, and its Methods section is more forthcoming about design compromises than most quantitative education papers. The problem is not obscurity -- it is that the argumentative voice of the paper (abstract, Introduction preview, Discussion) is consistently stronger and broader than the one reported table supports, and that several specific text-exhibit disagreements survived production. For readers, that means the paper's most-read sections are the least reliable, and the correct reading order is roughly the inverse of the printed one.

The most serious fidelity problem concerns endowments. Table 4 reports the endowment revenue ratio at 0.034 with a standard error of 0.026 and a marginal effect of 0.005 (SE 0.004) -- unambiguously null, and the Results paragraph correctly opens 'Financial factors appear to have limited influence.' But the same paragraph then adds that 'in a separate model excluding public/private control, the proportions of revenues derived from both tuition and government appropriations are negatively associated with having liberal speakers (statistically insignificant), whereas the endowment size is positively and significantly related to having liberal speakers.' That model is never shown. The two appendix tables the paper points to are the two-thirds-rule replication (A4) and the mixed-effects model (A5); neither is this. And the specification in question is obtained by deleting public/private control, which in Table 4 is by a wide margin the largest effect in the model (ME -0.186). Dropping the dominant institutional predictor and reporting that a correlated financial variable then turns significant is exactly the maneuver a reader would want flagged -- instead, the finding travels forward unqualified into the Introduction ('liberal speakers are more prevalent at larger institutions with more racially diverse student bodies and larger endowments') and the Discussion ('universities with more racially diverse student bodies and larger endowments tend toward liberal speakers'). To the paper's credit, the abstract does not repeat it. But a reader who reads only the abstract-plus-Discussion, which is most readers, ends with a belief the reported evidence contradicts.

The second serious problem is a direct self-contradiction in the description of the paper's central measure, and it is not a stylistic slip -- it changes what the paper's headline finding means. Page 14 states that the classification 'is based on each speaker's aggregated political donations between 1989 and 2024 and therefore does not capture potential changes in their political orientations over time.' The immediately following sentence begins 'Furthermore, because we measure political orientation using time-specific campaign contributions, our operationalization captures speakers' positioning relative to the political landscape at the moment of selection,' and then elaborates that a speaker classified liberal in 1995 reflects mid-1990s party alignment while one classified liberal in 2020 reflects contemporary dynamics. These are opposite claims about the same variable, joined by a connective ('Furthermore') that presents them as complementary -- the signature of a revision paragraph inserted without reconciling what preceded it. The stakes are high: RQ1 is entirely about change over time, and Figure 6 is the exhibit that answers it. If classification uses donations pooled across 36 years, then a 1991 speaker can be labeled on the basis of a 2016 contribution, and the observed post-2011 rise in liberal speakers may partly reflect the growth and partisan composition of the FEC donation record itself rather than changing invitation behavior. If classification is contemporaneous, the trend means what the paper says it means. The text does not let a reader decide, and neither reading can be ruled out from the Methods.

A related and under-flagged issue sits in the same neighborhood. The Results note in passing that 'the number of speakers with no political contributions also increased late in the study period.' Every trend analysis -- Figure 6, the piecewise regression, the 62% decomposition -- conditions on the 1,353 speakers whose orientation could be classified. If the unclassifiable share is growing, and growing non-randomly, the denominator of Figure 6 is shifting underneath the trend it displays. The paper raises the fact and drops it. It does the analogous check for the 'unique occupations' category, arguing from Figures 3 and 4 that their stable presence means 'their omission does not introduce systematic error' -- so the authors clearly understand the concern; they simply do not apply it to the category that, by their own account, is not stable.

On exhibit-text fidelity more locally, the arithmetic that can be checked mostly checks out, which is reassuring. Table 2 sums exactly: 1,043 + 310 + 233 + 91 + 163 + 35 = 1,875 under the 50% rule, and 1,019 + 291 + 43 + 233 + 91 + 163 + 35 = 1,875 under the two-thirds rule, with both proportion columns summing to 100.00. The text's '77% were liberal and 23% were conservative' is correct against the conditional denominator (1,043/1,353 = 77.1%, 310/1,353 = 22.9%), though a reader looking at Table 2 will see 55.63 and 16.53 in the Proportion column and must work out that the table conditions on 1,875 while the sentence conditions on 1,353 -- the table note explains the classification rules but not the denominators. Table 4's marginal effects are all the logit coefficient times a constant between 0.1517 and 0.1550, confirming they are a single-scale-factor transformation and adding no independent information; the same check exposes why percent Asian shows ME = 1.491, an impossible probability change arising from extrapolating a local derivative across a 0-to-1 range on a variable whose mean is 0.073. The text prudently never quotes that number, describing the race results only qualitatively -- but then the qualitative description ('greater proportions of minority students, particularly Hispanic and Asian') passes over that percent Black is 0.215 against SE 1.826, and that percent Hispanic clears only p < .10. The Discussion's compression of all this into 'more racially diverse student bodies' is the kind of generalization a reader should not repeat.

The enrollment sentence is a small but instructive case of unit drift. Table 4 gives ME = 0.047 per log unit; a 10% enrollment increase is 0.0953 log units, so the correct translation is 0.45 percentage points, not the 0.47% the text reports (the authors evidently multiplied by 0.1). The size of the error is trivial; the ambiguity around it is not, because the Results section uses '%' for percentage points throughout -- 18.6% for public control, 5.5% for urban location, 0.47% here -- and a reader who takes 18.6% as a relative change will badly understate an effect that is 18.6 points against a roughly 23% conservative base rate. The sentence also silently flips the outcome direction, describing a model of P(liberal) in terms of the likelihood of a conservative speaker. Elsewhere the terminology slips similarly: 0.399 is called a 'log odds ratio' when it is a log-odds coefficient, and the likelihood-ratio test justifying the choice of primary specification is rendered as 'likelihood ration = 1.71' -- a typo in the one sentence that carries the paper's model-selection decision.

The temporal claim, which is the abstract's first finding, deserves specific reader attention because of how it was constructed. The Methods describe observing 'a potential shift in temporal patterns around 2010,' then fitting a piecewise regression 'estimating the reflection point through the model-fitting process,' then reporting that 'the analysis confirmed a break point between 2010 and 2011.' The break is thus chosen from the data and then described with the language of confirmation. What is never reported is a test of whether the two segment slopes differ -- computing it by hand from the Figure 6 note (0.0121 vs 0.0010, SEs 0.0047 and 0.0022) gives t ~ 2.14, borderline, and that is before any penalty for having searched over break points. The abstract's 'particularly since 2011' and the Discussion's 'striking temporal pattern' both rest on this. Adjacent to it, the claim that the acceleration 'appears to align with an increase in speech disinvitation attempts from the left during the same period, as depicted in Figure 1' points at a figure captioned simply 'Number of campus speech disinvitation attempts over time' with a FIRE source note and no stated ideological decomposition; the reader cannot check the left/right split against the exhibit named.

The disinvitation results carry the paper's most consequential policy claim and its weakest disclosure. The Methods explain frankly that after applying a one-year lag, the authors 'tested various decay factors to assess how well this variable predicted commencement speakers' political ideologies' and that the analysis 'pointed to a decay factor of ~0.8.' That is a tuning parameter selected against the outcome, and the two coefficients it produces (0.129 and -0.183, both p < .05) inherit that selection. Nothing in the Results or Discussion revisits it. Instead the Discussion states that 'the evidence that disinvitation efforts influence institutional behavior suggests that speaker selection is more permeable to organized external pressure than is often acknowledged,' and derives from that a practical implication for university leaders about 'the degree to which platform allocation decisions reflect considered institutional judgment versus responsiveness to political mobilization.' Compounding this, at the sample means of the disinvitation variables (0.613 from the left, 0.237 from the right, per Table 3), the implied effects are on the order of one percentage point -- small in absolute terms and never contextualized against their own distributions. This is the single place in the paper where the gap between what was estimated and what is asserted is widest.

On organization: the shape is conventional and therefore easy to navigate, but the weighting is off for a reader's purposes. Roughly a third of the article precedes the data, and the Background, Theoretical Foundation, and Conceptualizing Political Orientation sections restate the same core proposition -- speaker selection as symbolic platform allocation conditioned by internal culture and external environment -- several times in successive paraphrases without narrowing it into testable expectations; there are no numbered hypotheses, so the reader arrives at Table 4 without a stated prior for any coefficient. The Results occupy about three pages and carry the entire empirical contribution. The Discussion is longer than the Results, and a large fraction of it is a future-research agenda (four explicit directions, plus a racialized-organization-theory extension) rather than interpretation of what was found. Most consequentially, there is no Limitations section at all. The genuine limitations -- non-random sampling, 28% of observations unclassifiable, a binary donation-based ideology proxy, no causal identification -- are real and mostly acknowledged, but they are dispersed across the Sample subsection, the Conceptualizing Political Orientation subsection, the Variables subsection, and a Table 4 note. A reader trying to assemble the case for caution has to visit four places, and the one limitation that matters most for how the abstract reads -- that nothing here supports causal language -- is never stated anywhere, in any section.

Finally, a cluster of small production lapses. Beyond 'likelihood ration = 1.71,' the Results paragraph on Figure 5 contains both 'focusing only the proportion' (missing preposition) and 'conversative speakers'; the citizen-ideology description refers to 'more liberal learnings of the state's general population'; the same passage attributes state-partisan-control data to the 'National State Council of Legislatures' where the paper elsewhere correctly cites the National Conference of State Legislatures; and the text cites 'Kors & Silvergate, 1999' against 'Silverglate' in the reference list. Individually these are trivial. Collectively, in a paper whose central problems are a null result reported as a finding, a measure described two contradictory ways, and a figure paragraph describing the wrong figure, they contribute to a reasonable reader's sense that the manuscript's final passes did not reconcile the prose against the exhibits.

The rating is 'adequate' rather than lower because the exposition is genuinely clear, the Methods disclosure is above average for the field, and the two exhibits that matter (Table 4 and the Figure 6 note) are self-contained enough that a diligent reader can recover the truth without the prose. It is not 'strong' because doing so requires the reader to correct the paper's own summary of itself in at least three places.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

Johnson and Zhang assemble a hand-built 35-year panel of 1,875 commencement speaker-institution-years at 52 U.S. universities, code each speaker's partisan orientation from FEC contribution records, and document both a post-2011 rise in liberal speakers and systematic cross-institutional variation — most notably that public institutions and institutions with heavier occupational/professional curricula invite conservative speakers more often. The data-construction effort and the descriptive time series are genuine and novel contributions with no close competitor. The interpretive apparatus — 'organizational platform allocation,' universities as 'strategic organizations navigating legitimacy,' disinvitation campaigns that 'influence' selection, and '62% of the time trend explained' — runs well ahead of what a pooled cross-sectional logistic model on a 52-institution convenience sample can establish.

**Strengths:**

- The dataset is the paper's real contribution: 1,875 speaker-institution-years across 52 institutions and 35 years, compiled by hand from institutional listings, archivists, and public relations officers, then matched individual-by-individual to FEC records on name, middle initial, employer, job title, and home address. Nothing comparable exists. Even readers who reject the paper's inferences inherit a new empirical object.
- The core descriptive fact — a flat partisan distribution through roughly 2010 (slope 0.0010, SE 0.0022) followed by a significant rise in liberal speakers (slope 0.0121, SE 0.0047), with the break point estimated rather than assumed — is a specific, dated, falsifiable claim that replaces impressionistic assertions about when campus platform politics shifted.
- The public/private gradient inverts the dominant popular narrative in a useful way. The 18.6 percentage-point higher probability of a conservative speaker at public institutions is the paper's largest and most stable estimate, and it reframes 'universities are liberal' as a claim that varies by sector rather than a property of higher education as such.
- The occupational/professional versus arts-and-sciences curricular gradient (marginal effect -0.230) is a genuinely fresh correlate. It connects speaker selection to Brint et al.'s long-running work on curricular change rather than to the usual faculty-ideology literature, and it is the kind of finding that would not have been guessed in advance.
- The paper moves the campus-speech literature from attitudinal and episodic evidence (surveys, interviews, case studies of individual controversies) to behavioral evidence on a routine, universally observed organizational practice. That shift in what counts as evidence is worth something independent of the specific estimates.
- The authors are candid about several limits: they explicitly disclaim speaker orientation as a proxy for institutional ideology, warn that the sample is not random, and name a substantial future-research agenda (qualitative work on how decisions are actually made, HBCUs and HSIs, other platform types, cross-national comparison) rather than implying the question is closed.

**Weaknesses:**

- The headline time trend is measured on a shrinking, non-random denominator. Only 1,353 of 1,875 observations (72%) are classifiable; 233 have no FEC record, 91 are foreign nationals, 163 hold 'unique occupations,' 35 are ambiguous. The paper itself notes that 'the number of speakers with no political contributions also increased late in the study period,' which means the composition of who enters Figures 5 and 6 changes across exactly the years the trend is measured. The trend and the attrition move together and the paper does not bound the resulting bias.
- The measurement instrument is itself non-stationary over the study window, and in a partisan-asymmetric direction. Individual federal donating changed enormously between 1989 and 2024 — the rise of online small-dollar giving, and ActBlue's disproportionate effect on the Democratic donor base in particular. A speaker with identical politics is far more likely to appear in FEC records as a Democratic donor in 2020 than in 1995. Some unknown share of the post-2011 'rise in liberal speakers' could be a rise in liberal-speaker detectability rather than a change in whom universities invite.
- The paper contradicts itself on how ideology is timed. One sentence states classification 'is based on each speaker's aggregated political donations between 1989 and 2024 and therefore does not capture potential changes in their political orientations over time'; the next paragraph states 'because we measure political orientation using time-specific campaign contributions, our operationalization captures speakers' positioning relative to the political landscape at the moment of selection.' These cannot both be true, and the second is the claim the discussion leans on.
- The '62% of the time trend explained' figure is close to mechanical. It comes from adding covariates and watching the year coefficient fall from 0.0044 to 0.0017. But the institutional covariates are time-invariant or slow-moving and cannot absorb a time trend; the variables that can are the state disinvitation counts, which themselves rise sharply over the same period (Figure 1). A trending regressor absorbing a trending year term is collinearity, not explanation. Readers should not cite 62% as an estimate of how much of the shift organizational and political factors 'drive.'
- The disinvitation result rests on a tuned parameter. The authors 'tested various decay factors to assess how well this variable predicted commencement speakers' political ideologies' and settled on ~0.8 — a parameter chosen by fitting to the outcome it is used to predict, without a stated theoretical basis or out-of-sample check. Combined with the collinearity above, the marginal effects (+0.020 for left-initiated, -0.028 for right-initiated) should be read as a description of two series moving together, not as evidence that campaigns changed behavior.
- Nothing in the design licenses the causal verbs the discussion uses. Every estimate in Table 4 is a cross-sectional association from a pooled logistic model; the mixed-effects specification with institution random intercepts is reported not to improve fit, and no fixed-effects specification is presented as primary. Yet the paper concludes that disinvitation efforts 'influence' selection, that speaker selection is 'permeable to organized external pressure,' and that universities are 'strategic organizations navigating legitimacy.' No decision process, no administrator, and no deliberation is observed anywhere in the data.
- Statistical precision is likely overstated for the institution-level predictors. Table 4 reports standard errors with no indication of clustering by institution, yet public/private, urbanicity, and selectivity are constant within institutions and vary across only 52 units, while N is 1,353. The strongest results (public institution, citizen ideology) would probably survive; the p < .05 and p < .10 findings — yield rate, urbanicity, Hispanic share, state party control, both disinvitation terms — are the ones most at risk.
- Some coefficients strain interpretation as reported. The percent-Asian marginal effect of 1.491 is a probability change greater than one, an artifact of scaling a proportion from 0 to 1 far outside the data's support (mean 0.073, SD 0.061); and the finding that urban and suburban institutions invite *more* conservative speakers (-0.055) runs against the paper's own theoretical logic and receives no discussion at all. Both suggest the covariate estimates are less settled than the discussion's confident enumeration implies.
- The sample cannot support level claims. It began as a convenience sample of institutions that happened to post speaker lists online, seeded from 20 AAU members plus 12 private baccalaureate colleges, and is acknowledged to be concentrated in the Northeast and along the coasts. It contains 4 public master's institutions, no community colleges, and no HBCUs or HSIs. The '77% liberal' figure is a property of this set of 52 institutions, not of American higher education.
- The theoretical contribution is largely nominal. 'Organizational platform allocation' renames a practice rather than generating a testable implication that distinguishes it from the publicity account, the ideological-composition account, or simple demand-side change in who is prominent in public life. The paper's own rebuttal of the publicity alternative — that publicity would predict uniform patterns across contexts — is weak, since the pool of nationally prominent, invitation-worthy figures plausibly shifted in composition over 35 years in ways that would produce cross-institutional variation without any organizational strategy at all.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- CITE IT FOR: the existence and shape of a 35-year descriptive series on commencement speaker partisanship, including the estimated 2010/2011 break point and the pre/post slopes. This is the paper's most durable contribution and there is no competing source.
- CITE IT FOR: the sector gradient — conservative speakers are substantially more common at public than private institutions in this sample (about 19 percentage points). It is the largest, most robust estimate in the paper and it usefully complicates the flat claim that 'universities platform liberals.'
- CITE IT FOR: the curricular gradient — institutions with larger occupational/professional enrollment shares invite fewer liberal speakers — as a novel correlate worth further study, stated as an association.
- CITE IT FOR: the methodological move itself, as an existence proof that speech-related organizational behavior can be studied with archival behavioral data rather than surveys and interviews.
- DO NOT CITE IT FOR: the claim that disinvitation campaigns influence or cause speaker selection. The disinvitation variable is a state-year count with a decay parameter tuned against the outcome, and it trends over time alongside the dependent variable — the association is not separable from the secular trend.
- DO NOT CITE IT FOR: the '62% of the time trend' figure. Coefficient attenuation from adding a covariate that trends in the same direction as time is not a variance-decomposition, and the number should not be read as the share of the shift attributable to organizational and political factors.
- DO NOT CITE IT FOR: the characterization of universities as 'strategic organizations navigating legitimacy.' No decision-making process is observed; this is an interpretive frame the authors bring to the correlations, and the paper's own future-research section concedes that qualitative work is needed to establish it.
- DO NOT CITE IT FOR: national or population estimates of the partisan composition of commencement speakers (the 77%/23% split). The 52-institution sample is a convenience-plus-purposive draw skewed toward AAU and coastal institutions, with no community colleges, almost no public master's institutions, and no HBCUs or HSIs.
- DO NOT CITE IT FOR: any claim about the ideology of non-donating public figures, or about clergy, judges, journalists, and military leaders (163 speakers), who are excluded by construction. Foreign speakers (91) are structurally unclassifiable.
- READ WITH CAUTION: the post-2011 rise itself. It is measured on the classifiable subsample only, and the unclassifiable share grows late in the period; separately, the propensity of any given individual to appear in FEC records as a Democratic donor rose sharply over the window for reasons unrelated to university behavior. The direction of the trend is probably real; its magnitude is not pinned down.
- OPEN QUESTIONS the paper leaves and names: who actually makes these decisions and how political risk enters the deliberation; whether continuous or issue-based ideology measures would reproduce the binary partisan patterns; whether the same dynamics govern speaker series, honorary degrees, and named lectureships; how platform allocation works at HBCUs and HSIs, which are absent here; and whether the concurrent rise in women and non-White speakers is a distinct process or the same one.
- STANDING: this is the best — effectively the only — systematic longitudinal evidence on its specific question, so it will and should become the default citation for the descriptive facts. Being uncontested is not the same as being well identified, and readers should cite the descriptive layer confidently and the explanatory layer as hypothesis.

**Detailed Commentary:**

What is genuinely new here separates cleanly from what is confirmatory, and readers should keep the two apart.

The genuinely new material is threefold. First, the data object: 1,875 speaker-institution-year observations at 52 institutions over 35 years, built by hand from institutional listings supplemented by correspondence with archivists and public relations officers, then matched person-by-person against FEC records using name, middle initial, employer, occupational history, and home address. This is unglamorous, expensive, non-automatable work, and it creates an empirical resource that did not previously exist in any form. Second, the descriptive time series with an estimated structural break: flat through roughly 2010 (slope 0.0010, SE 0.0022, indistinguishable from zero), then rising (slope 0.0121, SE 0.0047) from 2011 forward. The field has had impressions about when campus platform politics shifted; it now has a dated estimate located in a specific series. Third, the cross-institutional correlates, two of which are non-obvious: public institutions invite conservative speakers substantially more often than private ones, and institutions with larger occupational/professional enrollment shares invite fewer liberal speakers.

What is confirmatory is the headline the paper will most often be cited for — that universities invite more liberal than conservative speakers. The authors say so themselves: this is 'perhaps the least surprising finding.' Anyone who has read the faculty-ideology literature, or a newspaper, already believed it. The paper's value-add is not the level but the variance, and the sector inversion in particular is worth more than the aggregate split. Journalists and advocates will nonetheless quote the 77/23 number, which is exactly the figure the sample cannot support.

On the explanatory claims, there is a consistent gap between what the design delivers and what the discussion asserts. Every estimate in Table 4 is a cross-sectional association from a pooled logistic model; the mixed-effects specification is reported not to improve fit, and institution fixed effects are declined on the reasonable grounds that the theoretically central regressors are time-invariant. That is a defensible modeling choice, but it settles the question of what the estimates can mean: they are between-institution comparisons, adjusted for observables, on 52 units. From this the discussion concludes that disinvitation campaigns 'influence' selection, that speaker selection is 'more permeable to organized external pressure than is often acknowledged,' and that universities are 'strategic organizations navigating legitimacy under varying political conditions.' None of these is observed. No decision, deliberation, administrator, or selection committee appears anywhere in the data. The paper is inferring intent and process from an outcome distribution, and its own future-research section concedes as much when it calls for qualitative work on 'how speaker selection decisions are actually made.'

The disinvitation finding and the '62% explained' figure deserve particular scrutiny because they are the paper's most quotable and least supported claims, and they are entangled. Left-initiated disinvitation attempts in a state rise sharply after 2010 (the paper's own Figure 1); the proportion of liberal speakers rises sharply after 2011. Regressing the second on the first, with year also in the model, and then reporting that the year coefficient shrinks by 62% is a description of two collinear trends, not an explanation of one by the other. The institutional covariates cannot have done the absorbing — they are time-invariant or slow-moving by construction. The decay parameter compounds the problem: the authors report testing 'various decay factors to assess how well this variable predicted commencement speakers' political ideologies' and selecting ~0.8, which is a specification search over the outcome with no theoretical anchor and no held-out validation. Readers should treat the disinvitation coefficients as descriptive co-movement.

The measurement question is the one that most threatens even the descriptive contribution, and the paper does not engage it. Ideology is inferred from federal campaign contributions, but the propensity to make a recorded federal contribution changed dramatically between 1989 and 2024, and changed asymmetrically by party. The infrastructure of online small-dollar giving expanded the Democratic donor base disproportionately over precisely the post-2011 window where the paper locates its break. A public figure with fixed politics is simply more likely to be classifiable as liberal in 2020 than in 1995. Meanwhile the unclassifiable share grows late in the period — the paper notes that speakers with no contributions increase — so the denominator of Figures 5 and 6 shifts as the numerator does. The direction of the trend is plausibly real; its magnitude, and thus the '0.0121 per year' figure, is not pinned down. This also strains the theoretical bridge: a binary donation-derived partisan label is a thin instrument for claims about symbolic platform allocation, organizational identity, and racialized meaning-making. The paper is admirably careful about this in the conceptualization section and then largely forgets the caveat in the discussion.

Generalizability is bounded honestly in the methods and then overrun in the conclusion. The sample was seeded by which institutions posted speaker lists online, anchored on 20 AAU members plus 12 private baccalaureate colleges, and is visibly concentrated in the Northeast and on the coasts. It contains four public master's institutions, no community colleges (excluded on the grounds that they 'rarely have been sites of political contention over speech' — a defensible scoping choice, though it also excludes the sector enrolling the largest share of American undergraduates), and no HBCUs or HSIs, an omission the authors flag as future work while simultaneously invoking racialized organization theory to interpret the student-composition coefficients. The paper's defense — that the analysis relies on variation in institutional characteristics rather than regional representativeness — is fair for the internal comparisons but does not rescue the level estimates, and it understates the risk that a convenience sample of institutions willing to publicize decades of speaker history differs systematically in exactly the reputational-management dimension the paper theorizes about.

Precision is likely overstated for the very predictors the paper foregrounds. Public/private, urbanicity, admission rate, and yield are constant within institutions, so their effective sample size is 52, not 1,353. Table 4's note describes multiple imputation for citizen ideology (missing in about 20% of cases) but says nothing about clustering standard errors by institution. The two strongest results — public institution at p < .001 and citizen ideology at p < .001 — would probably survive; the yield rate, urbanicity, Hispanic share, state party control, and both disinvitation terms sit at p < .05 or p < .10 and are the natural casualties. Two coefficients also strain reading on their own terms: the percent-Asian marginal effect of 1.491 is a probability change exceeding one, produced by scaling a proportion whose mean is 0.073 across its full 0-to-1 range; and the finding that urban and suburban institutions invite more conservative speakers cuts against the paper's own framework and receives no discussion whatsoever. A reader should take the covariate table as a map of where to look next rather than as a set of settled magnitudes.

The theoretical reframing is the weakest layer. 'Organizational platform allocation' is a name for something the field could already point at, and it is not developed into an implication that would distinguish it empirically from the alternatives. The paper does try — it argues that if publicity drove selection, patterns would be uniform across organizational contexts — but this rebuttal assumes the pool of prominent, invitation-worthy public figures held constant in composition over 35 years, which is exactly what did not happen. The rise of women and non-White speakers alongside liberal speakers, which the authors report in appendix figures and flag as unexplained, is consistent with a demand-side story in which the population of nationally prominent figures changed while institutional strategy did not. The organizational-culture and resource-dependency framings are invoked to interpret coefficients but are never placed in a position where they could have been rejected.

On standing: within its narrow question this is now the reference, and will be cited as such. That reflects the absence of competitors as much as the strength of the evidence. Its most likely misuse is predictable — the '77% liberal' figure lifted into campus-speech policy debates as a national statistic, and the disinvitation coefficients read as proof that activist pressure moves institutional behavior. Both would be misuses. The right posture is to treat the descriptive series and the sector and curricular gradients as findings, the environmental correlations as hypotheses, and the organizational-strategy narrative as an interpretive frame awaiting the qualitative and design-based work the authors themselves call for. Rated adequate: a real and effortful empirical contribution to a question that matters, with a genuinely novel dataset and one counterintuitive result, paired with an explanatory apparatus that outruns its evidence in the sections readers quote most.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

Johnson and Zhang name every data source they use and, unusually for a hand-built dataset, report publishing the underlying speaker list in the online appendix, and their exclusion ledger (Table 2) accounts for all 1,875 observations without slippage. But the article carries no data availability statement, no replication package, and no code, and its central measurement step — hand-matching 1,875 speakers to FEC contribution records — is described only narratively, with no matching algorithm, thresholds, reliability check, or published classification. Several downstream choices (a tuned 0.8 decay factor, the multiple-imputation model, the piecewise breakpoint search, the treatment of standard errors) are stated but not specified, so the headline results are legible in their logic yet not practically verifiable as reported.

**Strengths:**

- Every data source is named and publicly accessible: FEC individual-contribution records, IPEDS institutional characteristics/enrollment/finance surveys, NCSL state party control, Berry et al. (2007) citizen ideology, and the FIRE campus deplatforming database. Nothing is restricted-use, so there is no legal barrier to a full replication — the barriers are all documentary.
- The exclusion accounting is complete and internally consistent, which is rare and directly checkable. Table 2's categories (1,043 liberal + 310 conservative + 233 no contribution + 91 foreign + 163 unique occupation + 35 unclear) sum exactly to 1,875, the percentages reproduce to the reported decimal, the two-thirds-rule column sums to the same 1,353 classified speakers, and the regression N = 1,353 in Table 4 matches the classified total. A reader can trace the sample from raw observations to estimation sample without guessing.
- The authors report having published the speaker roster itself (Appendix Tables A2 and A3, the latter listing all 1,485 unique speakers and their address counts). For a dataset assembled by hand from institutional websites and archivists, releasing the underlying list rather than only aggregates is a meaningful transparency choice and is the single thing that keeps this study within reach of replication.
- Sampling is described candidly rather than dressed up: the two-stage convenience-then-purposive design is disclosed as non-random, the resulting tilt toward well-resourced and coastal institutions is acknowledged, and the full 52-institution list is in Appendix Table A1, so readers can see exactly which institutions carry the findings.
- Several analytic choices that authors often leave implicit are stated plainly: time-invariant covariates (control, location, admission and yield rates) are taken from the 2022 IPEDS files and applied across all years; a one-year lag is applied to the disinvitation variable with an explicit rationale; the tie-break rule for institutions that moved to college-level ceremonies (take the largest college) is given; and the software and specific commands (Stata's mi estimate, the user-written mimrgns) are named.
- Robustness checks are pre-specified and located: the two-thirds classification rule (Appendix Table A4) and the mixed-effects logit with institution random intercepts (Appendix Table A5) are both reported rather than merely asserted, with the likelihood-ratio comparison stated in the text.

**Weaknesses:**

- No data availability statement, no replication package, no posted code, and no data citation with an accession identifier or access date for any of the five secondary sources. For a 2026 AERJ article using entirely public inputs, this falls short of current journal-era norms; the Supplemental Material note says only that supplemental material is available online.
- The FEC name-matching procedure — the study's core measurement — is not reproducible from the description. The paper says matching involved comparing last name, first name, middle initial, and occupational history against all FEC records 1989–2024, with home-address confirmation when discrepancies arose. No matching rule, string-distance or blocking method, decision threshold, double-coding, or inter-rater reliability is reported, and the boundary between the 233 speakers ruled out as absent from FEC and the 35 judged 'unclear' rests on unstated judgments about name distinctiveness.
- The classification of each speaker is apparently not published. Appendix Table A3 is described as listing the 1,485 unique speakers and their number of addresses, with no ideology column mentioned; A2 is described in a way ('most institutions hosted a single commencement speaker each year') more consistent with a count distribution than a name-level institution-year roster. If neither table carries the speaker-by-institution-by-year mapping with its assigned category, the analytic spine cannot be rebuilt and none of Figures 3–6 or Tables 2–4 is checkable without redoing the entire hand-coding.
- The measurement window for contributions is internally contradictory. The text states the classification 'is based on each speaker's aggregated political donations between 1989 and 2024 and therefore does not capture potential changes in their political orientations over time,' then states two sentences later that 'because we measure political orientation using time-specific campaign contributions, our operationalization captures speakers' positioning relative to the political landscape at the moment of selection.' A replicator cannot tell whether the variable is a lifetime aggregate or a time-localized share, and these produce different data.
- The blend of the two ideology sources is undocumented. Party affiliation is used for elected officials and FEC shares for everyone else, but the paper never reports how many of the 1,353 classified speakers come from each route, what rule applies when an elected official also has FEC records that point the other way, or how party affiliation was determined (and for which offices) — with no source cited for the officeholder party data at all.
- The 0.8 decay factor for cumulative disinvitation pressure was selected by testing 'various decay factors to assess how well this variable predicted commencement speakers' political ideologies' — that is, tuned against the dependent variable. The candidate grid, the fit criterion, the results across candidates, and any sensitivity to the choice are all unreported, and the exact construction (how the one-year lag composes with the decayed cumulative sum) cannot be reconstructed from the text or from the descriptives.
- The multiple-imputation model is unspecified. Citizen ideology is missing for roughly 20% of cases and 20 imputations are run via mi estimate, but the imputation method (mvn versus chained equations), the variables entering the imputation model, whether the outcome was included, the random seed, and the reason for the missingness are all absent. Since the Berry et al. series ends before 2024, the missingness is likely concentrated in the final years — precisely the period driving the post-2011 acceleration — but the paper never says so.
- The treatment of standard errors is never stated. Table 4's note says only 'Standard errors are reported in parentheses.' With 1,353 observations nested in 52 institutions (roughly 26 apiece), state-year covariates shared across institutions in a state, and speakers who recur many times (Marian Wright Edelman appears 13 times), non-independence is severe on at least three dimensions, yet no clustering is mentioned. The mixed-effects model in Appendix Table A5 addresses only the institution dimension, and its comparison test is reported as 'likelihood ration = 1.71; p > .05' without degrees of freedom or a note on the boundary (chibar2) issue.
- Two sets of results appear only in prose with no table anywhere. The claim that the model 'accounts for about 62% of the observed time trend' rests on a specification with a year term plus covariates that is not shown (Table 4 contains no year variable), and the 'separate model excluding public/private control' in which endowment becomes positive and significant is likewise unreported. Neither is regenerable, and neither is flagged as appendix material.
- Specification details needed to re-run Table 4 are missing: whether the state party control and citizen ideology variables are contemporaneous or lagged (disinvitations are explicitly lagged one year on a selection-timing rationale that would apply equally to the other state variables), whether year or region terms are included, the coding of Nebraska's nonpartisan unicameral legislature in the 0/0.5/1 party-control scale, and the CIP-to-category crosswalk behind 'percent occupational/professional majors,' which is attributed to Brint et al. (2005) but not reproduced.
- No harmonization is described for 35 years of IPEDS. The finance variables span the GASB/FASB reporting change of the early 2000s and the finance-survey redesign, and the race/ethnicity categories changed with the 2010 introduction of the two-or-more-races category — all of which affect the enrollment-composition and revenue-share covariates. The paper reports the variables as if the series were continuous.
- Panel completeness is never reported. Fifty-two institutions across 1989–2024 imply about 1,872 institution-years; the paper observes 1,875 speaker-institution-years, some years carrying two or three speakers and 2020–21 carrying none, and stage-one institutions were included on the basis of 'complete or partial' online lists. The number of institution-years with no recovered speaker, and whether coverage is thinner in the early period, are not disclosed — which matters because uneven coverage over time could partly generate the headline trend.
- The NCSL citation does not match the variable it supports. The reference list points to NCSL's education legislation bill-tracking database, not to NCSL's state partisan composition tables, and the text names the agency as the 'National State Council of Legislatures.' A replicator following the citation lands on the wrong file.
- Reporting gaps in the exhibits themselves: Table 4 gives no pseudo-R-squared, log-likelihood, AIC/BIC, or number of institutions/clusters, and the units of the marginal effects are unstated — the reported effects for percent Hispanic (0.817) and percent Asian (1.491) exceed the probability scale, which only makes sense as a full 0-to-1 shift in a proportion, and readers must infer that. No model-fit statistics are provided for the piecewise regression in Figure 6, no confidence interval or search method is given for the estimated breakpoint, and the post-2011 slope's p-value is not adjusted for the fact that the breakpoint was estimated from the same data.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Before citing the ideology series as a measure, download Appendix Table A3 and check whether it carries a classification column. If it lists only names and address counts, treat every ideology-based number in the paper — Table 2, Figures 3, 5, and 6, and all of Table 4 — as taken on trust: nothing downstream of the FEC hand-match is independently checkable without redoing the match.
- Check whether Appendix Table A2 gives speaker names by institution and year or only counts per institution-year. This single fact determines whether the dataset's spine is public. If it is a name-level roster, the study is close to fully replicable from public files; if it is a count distribution, it is not.
- Ask the authors directly for the analytic dataset and do-files, and specifically for: the FEC matching protocol and match-rate diagnostics, the imputation model and seed, the decay-factor search results, and the two prose-only regressions (the year-plus-covariates model behind the 62% claim and the model dropping public/private control that makes endowment significant). None of these can be reconstructed from the article.
- Do not rely on the reported significance levels in Table 4 without clarification on clustering. The note is silent, and the plausible readings — unclustered, clustered by institution, or clustered by state — differ materially with 52 institutions, state-level regressors, and speakers recurring up to 13 times. The marginal results in particular (state party control at p < .10; location, yield rate, occupational majors, and both disinvitation variables at p < .05) are the ones most likely to move.
- Treat the disinvitation coefficients as the least verifiable estimates in the paper. The variable's decay parameter was selected on how well it predicted the outcome, the search was not reported, and no sensitivity analysis across decay values is offered — so the left/right disinvitation effects should be read as suggestive pending an independent reconstruction at alternative decay values, including 0 (pure one-year lag) and 1 (undecayed cumulative).
- Resolve the aggregation-window contradiction before treating the ideology measure as time-varying. The paper's own text supports both a lifetime aggregate and a time-localized share; if the measure is in fact a lifetime aggregate, then the interpretive claim that classifications reflect 'positioning at the moment of selection' does not hold, and the time trend is a trend in the composition of speakers rather than in the political landscape they are read against.
- Interrogate panel completeness before leaning on the temporal findings. Ask what fraction of the 52 institutions have a recovered speaker in each year, and whether coverage improves after 2010. Because the headline result is a post-2011 acceleration in liberal share, differential coverage by era is a live alternative explanation the article does not foreclose.
- For anyone attempting a replication: the covariate side is genuinely feasible — IPEDS, Berry et al. citizen ideology, FIRE's deplatforming database, and NCSL partisan composition (not the education bill-tracking database the reference list cites) are all downloadable. The outcome side is where a replication will stall, and a partial replication that rebuilds the covariates and re-estimates on the authors' classifications, if obtained, is the realistic path.
- When citing the exclusion decisions, note that the 163 'unique occupation' exclusions (military, clergy, judges, media) rest on a coding boundary the paper never defines. That category is nearly 9% of observations and includes occupations with plausible partisan skew in both directions, so readers should treat the authors' stability argument (Figure 4) as evidence about counts, not about ideological composition.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Transparency in this paper is a story of good sources and thin documentation. Every input is public and every input is named: FEC individual-contribution records, IPEDS institutional characteristics, enrollment, and finance surveys, NCSL state party control, the Berry et al. (2007) citizen ideology series, and FIRE's campus deplatforming database. There is no restricted-use data, no data-use agreement, no privacy constraint — nothing that would legitimately prevent a full replication package. That matters for how the reproducibility gaps should be read: they are not the unavoidable cost of working with administrative microdata, which the domain routinely and properly excuses. They are choices, and in a 2026 AERJ article they sit against journal-era expectations of a data availability statement, a deposited package, and a documented software environment. The article's only relevant note reads that supplemental material is available online.

What is genuinely verifiable deserves credit first. The exclusion ledger in Table 2 is complete and arithmetically clean: 1,043 liberal, 310 conservative, 233 with no contributions, 91 foreign nationals, 163 in 'unique occupations,' and 35 unclear sum precisely to the 1,875 speaker-institution-year observations, the reported percentages reproduce, the two-thirds-rule column sums to the same 1,353 classified speakers, and the 1,353 carries through to the estimation sample in Table 4. A reader can follow the sample from raw observations to regression N without a single unexplained drop — an ordinary virtue that is nonetheless frequently absent. The 52-institution list is in Appendix Table A1, the sampling design is described as non-random and its likely tilt acknowledged, the time-invariant covariates are explicitly pinned to the 2022 IPEDS files, the disinvitation lag is stated with a rationale, the tie-break rule for split ceremonies is given, and the software and commands are named down to the user-written mimrgns. Most consequentially, the authors report publishing the speaker roster itself in Appendix Table A3 — for a dataset assembled by hand from institutional websites and archivists over 35 years, releasing the list rather than only aggregates is the choice that keeps replication conceivable at all.

The decisive question, which I cannot answer from the main text alone, is what the appendix tables actually contain. Table A3 is described as 'a list of the 1,485 unique speakers in our sample and the number of commencement addresses they delivered' — names and counts, with no ideology column mentioned. Table A2 is invoked to support the claim that 'most institutions hosted a single commencement speaker each year,' phrasing more consistent with a distribution of speaker counts than with a name-level institution-year roster. If that reading is right, then the two things a replicator most needs — the speaker-to-institution-to-year mapping, and each speaker's assigned political category — are not published, and the entire chain from Table 2 through Figures 3, 5, and 6 to Table 4 rests on a hand-coding step no one outside the author team can inspect. If instead A2 is a full roster and A3 carries classifications, the study is close to fully replicable from public files, and I would rate it adequate or better. Readers should check this before deciding how much weight the ideology series can bear.

The FEC matching procedure is where reproducibility fails most clearly regardless of what the appendix holds. The paper describes 'a laborious process in which we compared the last name, first name, middle initial, and occupational history of commencement speakers with all FEC records between 1989 and 2024,' with home-address confirmation used to resolve discrepancies. That is an honest account of what was done, but it is not a protocol. There is no blocking or string-distance method, no match threshold, no double-coding or inter-rater reliability, and no diagnostics on match rates by era or speaker type. The classification also blends two sources — party affiliation for elected officials, FEC contribution shares for everyone else — without reporting how many speakers came from each route, without citing a source for the officeholder party data, and without stating the rule when an officeholder's own contributions point away from their party. And the measurement window is stated two ways within a single paragraph: first as an aggregate of 'political donations between 1989 and 2024' that 'does not capture potential changes in their political orientations over time,' then as 'time-specific campaign contributions' capturing 'positioning at the moment of selection.' These are different variables. A replicator would have to pick one and hope.

A second cluster of gaps concerns tuned or unspecified analytic parameters. The disinvitation decay factor of approximately 0.8 was chosen by testing candidate values 'to assess how well this variable predicted commencement speakers' political ideologies' — selection on the dependent variable, with the grid, criterion, results, and sensitivity all unreported, and the composition of the one-year lag with the decayed cumulative sum left to inference. The multiple imputation covering roughly 20% missingness on citizen ideology reports only the command and the number of imputations: no method, no variables in the imputation model, no seed, and no account of why the data are missing. Since the Berry et al. series does not extend to 2024, the missingness is very likely concentrated at the end of the panel — the same years that drive the paper's central post-2011 finding — and the paper does not raise this. The piecewise regression that establishes the 2010–2011 breakpoint says the reflection point was estimated 'through the model-fitting process' with no method named, no confidence interval on the breakpoint, and no acknowledgment that the post-2011 slope's p-value is conditional on a breakpoint chosen from the same data.

Specification transparency for Table 4 is partial. The covariate list is legible and the descriptives in Table 3 let a reader check scaling, but several things needed to re-run the model are absent: whether state party control and citizen ideology are contemporaneous or lagged (the authors lag disinvitations on a selection-timing argument that applies with equal force to the other state variables, and then do not apply it), whether any year or region terms enter, how Nebraska's nonpartisan unicameral legislature is coded on the 0/0.5/1 scale, and what CIP crosswalk implements the occupational-versus-arts-and-sciences split attributed to Brint et al. (2005). Nothing is said about harmonizing IPEDS across the GASB/FASB accounting transition or the 2010 race-category revision, both of which fall inside the 35-year window and both of which affect covariates the paper interprets substantively. The standard-error treatment is simply not stated — the table note says only that standard errors are in parentheses — even though the data are non-independent along at least three dimensions (institution, state-year, and repeat speakers, one of whom appears 13 times). The mixed-effects specification in Appendix Table A5 speaks to the institution dimension only, and its comparison is reported as 'likelihood ration = 1.71; p > .05' with no degrees of freedom and no note on the variance-component boundary problem.

Finally, results reporting leaves two claims outside the exhibit structure entirely. The statement that the model 'accounts for about 62% of the observed time trend' (marginal effect of year falling from 0.0044 to 0.0017) requires a specification containing a year term, and Table 4 contains none; the corresponding post-2011 calculation (0.0121 to 0.0066) is likewise from an unreported model. So too is the 'separate model excluding public/private control' in which endowment size becomes positively and significantly associated with liberal speakers — a finding echoed in the abstract and discussion but shown nowhere. Neither is flagged as appendix material. Table 4 itself omits pseudo-R-squared, log-likelihood, information criteria, and the number of institutions, and does not state the units of the marginal effects, which is why the reported values for percent Hispanic (0.817) and percent Asian (1.491) run past the probability scale and must be silently read as full 0-to-1 shifts in a proportion. One smaller but concrete citation problem compounds the difficulty: the reference given for state party control is NCSL's education legislation bill-tracking database, not its state partisan composition tables, and the agency is named in-text as the 'National State Council of Legislatures.' A replicator following the citation retrieves the wrong file.

On balance I rate this weak rather than adequate, and I want to be explicit that it sits near the boundary. The sources are transparent, the sample accounting is exemplary, and the authors have gone further than most hand-coding studies by putting a speaker list in the public record. But the study's central variable is produced by an unspecified manual process whose output does not appear to be published; the parameter governing the disinvitation results was tuned against the outcome without disclosure; the imputation model, the breakpoint search, and the standard-error treatment are all unstated; two reported findings have no exhibit; and there is no package, no code, and no data availability statement despite the complete absence of any legal or ethical barrier to providing them. A determined replicator could rebuild the covariate side of this study from public files in a few weeks. Rebuilding the outcome side would mean redoing 1,875 hand-matches against a protocol that has not been written down, and would produce a different dataset. That is the practical meaning of the rating: the paper's descriptive picture and its associations are plausible and internally coherent, but as published they are checkable only by taking the measurement on trust.
